search_result.text:
Danielle Dreilinger

The American South

Dec. 13, 2022, 3:30 a.m. ET

When the lights snapped out at the drag show in Moore County, North Carolina, the producers and performers thought: This was unlikely to be a coincidence.

As of Dec. 8, authorities were still investigating the attack on two substations, which took out power for about 45,000 people for four days. They haven’t found any evidence it was tied to the show.

search_result.title: Hawk Fire Sunday updates: 15K acres - Reno Gazette Journal
search_result.text:
Aug. 23, 2026 Updated Aug. 24, 2026, 10:04 a.m. ET

For Hawk Fire updates on Monday, Aug. 24, click here.

The Hawk Fire has grown to more than 15,000 acres, prompting expanded evacuation orders across northwest Reno and the North Valleys. Approximately close to 90,000 residents live within the mandatory evacuation and evacuation warning zones.

The fire was listed at 0% containment as of 11 a.m. Sunday. Officials confirmed structures were lost, though the number and types of structures were not immediately available.

Public safety officials have established an information line for the Hawk Fire at 775-244-6988. Information is also available at facebook.com/HawkFire2026.

Here's what we know Sunday:

How to report suspected price gouging during Hawk Fire

For anyone who thinks they’ve experienced price gouging tied to the Hawk Fire, the Nevada attorney general’s office urges them to fill out a formal complaint so it can investigate.

This might include renting a motel or hotel room, buying food and water, or even boarding a pet.

Nevada law considers price gouging at three levels. For goods or services valued up to $250, one cannot sell them for more than 15% of the usual prices. From $250 to $750, the restriction is no more than 10% higher, and for more than $750, it’s a max of 5% higher.

The price gouging ban lasts through the time the state emergency or disaster is in effect, or until 75 days, whichever comes first.

Details on filing a complaint and a link to the online form can be found at https://ag.nv.gov/Complaints/CSU_Complaints___FAQ.

Hawk Fire power outages peaked at 60,000 customers

At the peak of fire activity for the Hawk Fire on Saturday, about 60,000 customers were out of power, according to Jesse Murray, NV Energy senior vice president. The outages included customers who were “well beyond the immediate fire impact area,” Murray said.

“The reason for that is we had several critical transmission facilities in the area that were directly impacted by the fire, which means those outages often have to expand much beyond that fire zone so that we can maintain grid stability,” Murray said.

“So that’s why we saw those numbers as high as they were.”

By early Sunday, the number of NV Energy customers without power was down 10,000. Murray attributed the reduction to its crew members’ efforts as well as favorable weather conditions overnight.

The 10,000 customers are primarily located in the Silver Lake, Stead, and Lemon Valley areas.

NV Energy also has about 250 gas customers who were out of service as of noon on Sunday. All of the affected gas customers are located south and west of US 395.

Hawk Fire grows to more than 15,000 acres

The Hawk Fire has grown to more than 15,000 acres, according to a new fire perimeter from the National Interagency Fire Center.

The latest perimeter lists the fire at 15,040 acres, up from approximately 13,000 acres reported by fire officials Sunday morning.

Washoe County jail has not been evacuated from Hawk Fire, sheriff says

Washoe County’s top law enforcement official confirmed that the county’s detention facility has not been evacuated due to the Hawk Fire, but added that they continue to monitor the situation and will be ready to go should the wildfire worsen.

“We have not evacuated anybody,” Sheriff Darin Balaam said during a Sunday press conference about the Hawk Fire. “We have just made the initial phone calls and have everybody on standby.”

The Washoe County Detention Center is located at 911 Parr Blvd., in Reno, which remains outside of currently established evacuation zones as of Sunday afternoon.

The sheriff’s office, however, has made contingency plans should the fire draw closer to the county jail.

Personnel from the sheriff’s office as well as other entities are on standby to assist in the event of an evacuation, according to Balaam. The contingencies include arranging treatment for inmates who need care.

“For those that have loved ones in our detention facility, we have their safety as our number one priority,” Balaam said.

“So if we have to evacuate the jail, we will get your loved ones out. We will send them to other facilities around the surrounding areas or hospitals if they have medical needs that we need to take care of.”

Some areas west of North Virginia Street are currently within the red “go now” evacuation zones. Other areas east of Virginia Street such as Bonanza Casino, which is just a mile away from the detention center, are within the yellow “get ready” evacuation zone as of Sunday afternoon.

WCSD, TMCC classes canceled Monday due to Hawk Fire

Classes have been canceled for nearly all Washoe County School District schools Monday due to the effects of the Hawk Fire, and Truckee Meadows Community College will be closed as well.

Parents of WCSD students were alerted via phone calls, texts and emails shortly after noon on Sunday.

"The decision to close schools is due to evacuations, impacts on regional public safety resources, and to help keep roads clear for emergency vehicles," the message read.

Schools in Gerlach will hold classes as scheduled.

WCSD officials consulted with local law enforcement and public safety officials on the decision; the district cited strain on public safety and transit as crews continue to battle the fire.

"We understand that so many people in our WCSD family — students, families, and staff — are impacted," the message continued. "Over the next few days, we will continue to update our entire district family with information as it becomes available. We are grateful to our firefighters and first responders as they continue to battle this fire, and we thank our district personnel who are assisting with this effort."

TMCC also canceled campus operations for Monday, including both in-person and remote classes, on what would have been the first day of instruction for the fall semester.

"Our thoughts are with everyone affected by the Hawk Fire and the extraordinary impact it is having across our region," the statement read. "With approximately 42,000 residents currently evacuated and another 45,000 residents in the evacuation warning areas, we know that many members of our TMCC community may be facing uncertainty, displacement or concern for family, friends, and neighbors."

TMCC's campus at 7000 Dandini Boulevard is about one-half mile east of an evacuation warning zone.

The University of Nevada, Reno, confirmed that it will continue ahead with its first day of class.

“Following an assessment of the Hawk Fire and current smoke conditions in the vicinity of the University of Nevada, Reno, the University has determined that regular campus operations will continue on Monday, Aug. 24,” UNR announced in a statement.

“Classes and operations at the University's main campus, Redfield campus and Lake Tahoe campus will proceed as scheduled.”

UNR added that it remains safe and is not located in either a red or yellow evacuation zone. The university also has an emergency response plan in place should the wildfire threaten the school.

“University leadership will continue to closely monitor fire activity, air quality conditions and guidance from local authorities, and will provide additional updates as needed,” UNR said.

Hawk Fire confirmed as human caused; 6 injured and 13,000 acres burned

The Reno area is grappling with another wildfire that was sparked by human hands, officials confirmed during a press event on Sunday morning.

“We can confirm that the fire was human caused,” said Shane Akerson, a battalion chief with the Truckee Meadows Fire Protection District.

“However, that is still undergoing active investigation and we don’t have further details provided at this time.”

Akerson also confirmed that the fire has grown from 10,500 acres late Saturday to approximately 13,000 acres as of early Sunday.

At least six injuries have been injured from the Hawk Fire so far — three civilians and three first responders, according to Akerson.

While officials confirmed that structures have been burned in the fire, they were unable to provide an exact count because the sites are not safe yet for investigators to enter.

About 800 personnel are working on the Hawk Fire as of Sunday morning, Akerson said.

The number of potentially affected residents by the Hawk Fire currently stands just under 90,000 people.

“Currently, we have 42,000 individuals who are placed on active evacuation, with approximately 45,000 individuals that are in the set status to be prepared to be evacuated,” Akerson said.

Grace Church providing food, water to firefighters, evacuees during Hawk Fire

Grace Church canceled their Sunday services to provide food, water and Gatorade for evacuees and firefighters as the Hawk Fire continues to burn in northwest Reno.

"We were going to assemble them after church today," said Shane Marks, lead pastor of Grace Church, but church leaders opted to forgo its services and begin distribution earlier than planned.

"The church is rallying," Marks told the RGJ.

The church at 1220 Robb Drive is in a neighborhood currently designated as an evacuation warning zone.

Hundreds at shelter; hotshot teams from California battling Hawk Fire

Hundreds of residents of northwest Reno and the North Valleys stayed at shelters Saturday night, the Northern Nevada Chapter of the American Red Cross reported.

Shelter space continues to be available at the Reno-Sparks Convention Center, Hall 4, at 4590 S. Virginia Street.

"The overnight count of people in the shelter was 469 people, with more than 200 others choosing to stay in their cars, campers and RVs in the parking lot and still having access to the shelter services," Keith Paul, regional communications director with the Red Cross, told the RGJ. "There is still room and if needed, we can expand the current shelter or open another one."

California hotshot crews are on the front lines fighting the Hawk Fire, an RGJ journalist reported from the scene.

Nevada Sen. Jacky Rosen is looking at potential options from the federal level to help with the Hawk Fire.

“This is a very dangerous situation that is evolving quickly,” Rosen posted on X.com, formerly Twitter.

“I’m in touch with local officials to see what federal resources could be needed as first responders work around the clock to fight this fire.”

Here are the latest evacuation zones for the Hawk Fire in Reno

Here is a roundup of neighborhoods located in evacuation zones for the Hawk Fire based on the latest information available as of 10 a.m. Sunday.

RED “GO NOW” EVACUATION ZONE

Areas around Somersett Parkway, including Sierra Vista Park, Canyon Golf, Somersett Golf and Country Club, and Somersett West Park.

Areas around the northern portion of Robb Drive and northwest of Mae Anne Avenue, including McQueen High School, Northwest Reno Library, Rollan D. Melton Elementary School, George Westergard Elementary School, Valley Wood Park.

Areas around Las Brisas Boulevard, the northern portion of King Row north of North McCarran Boulevard, and north of West Seventh Street from Robb Drive to North McCarran Boulevard.

Rancho San Rafael Regional Park and the Reno Sports Complex.

The area around Hoge Road west of North Virginia Street, including Bonanza Terrace RV Park and the western portion of Rancho San Rafael Townhomes.

The Raleigh Heights neighborhood around North Virginia Street and West Golden Valley Road.

The area around Beckwourth Drive, including Alice Smith Elementary School and the the North Hills Shopping Center, which has North Valleys Library and a Raley’s grocery store.

The area around U.S. Highway 395 from Lemmon Drive to Village Parkway, including the Sky Vista Parkway Walmart and Smith’s, North Valleys Regional Park, Country Terrace Mobile Village, Stead Elementary School, O’Brian Middle School, Sierra Sage Golf Course, Silver Lake and White Lake.

Resources from Bug, Stallion fires assisting with Hawk Fire

While fire crews battle the Hawk Fire, they're still working to contain two wildfires still burning in northwestern Nevada: the Bug Fire, burning since Aug. 8; and the Stallion Fire, burning since Aug. 10.

The Bug Fire is currently listed at 93,733 acres and is at 94% containment. The Stallion Fire is at 40,691 acres and 98% containment.

The FireNet Resource Center reported Sunday morning that resources from those fires are assisting with the Hawk Fire as needed. Two crews with a total of 202 personnel continue to battle the two fires. Three helicopters and six engines and water tenders are in use.

“With the new Hawk Fire incident in the region, resources from Bug and Stallion are currently assisting as needed, including both helicopter aviation assets,” the incident team for both fires said in a statement.

“As the Bug and Stallion Fires move further into recovery, the focus remains on initial attack response, completing suppression repair, and safely returning impacted areas to the community.”

Here is an updated list of the latest road closures from the Hawk Fire in Reno

Officials and emergency crews continue to advise motorists to stay away from designated evacuation zones as the Hawk Fire reaches its second day.

Reno City Council member Devon Reese advised residents not to return to closed evacuation areas until they are officially reopened.

“Conditions are expected to be critical,” Reese said in a Facebook post. “If you are in a warning zone, do not wait for the wind to shift before you get ready.”

The Washoe County Sheriff’s Office also released a list of the latest road closures from the Hawk Fire.

Here is road closure information for U.S. Highway 395 as of Sunday morning:

Northbound US 395 is closed from Parr Boulevard to Red Rock Road.

Southbound US 395 traffic at Bordertown is being turned around before reaching White Lake.

Southbound US 395 remains open from Red Rock Road south into Reno.

Here are the current road closures in the Reno area from the Hawk Fire.

U.S. 395 at Bordertown

U.S. 395 at Village Parkway

U.S. 395 at White Lake Parkway

North Virginia Street at White Lake Parkway

Northbound US 395 at Red Rock Road

Southbound US 395 at Stead Boulevard

Stead Boulevard at Matthews Street

North Virginia Street at Panther Drive

North Virginia Street at Parr Boulevard

North Virginia Street at East Golden Valley Road

Mae Anne Avenue at Somersett Parkway

Del Webb Parkway at Somersett Parkway

Robb Drive at Los Brisas Boulevard

Lemmon Valley Drive at North Virginia Street

Golden Vista Avenue at North Hills Boulevard

East Golden Valley Road at Beckwourth Drive

Red Rock Road at North Virginia Street

Stead Boulevard at North Virginia Street

Sharlands Avenue at Mae Anne Avenue

Beaumont Parkway at Avenida de Landa

Red Flag Warning ended, light winds in forecast

Gov. Joe Lombardo declared a state of emergency in Washoe County. About 400 local, state and federal personnel are assigned to the incident, including ground crews and air resources.

About 10 air resources were ordered and are set to start attacking the Hawk Fire today at 8:30 a.m., according to Reno City Council member Devon Reese.

More than 10,000 NV Energy customers remain without power in Washoe County as of noon Sunday.

Fire officials said strong, gusty winds, low humidity and dry vegetation fueled the fire’s significant growth.

An area of about 75 square miles remained under mandatory evacuation orders. Orders include parts of Somersett and neighborhoods north of West Seventh Street to North McCarran Boulevard. Residents should check perimetermap.com for exact boundaries and current road closures.

The fire started about 11:30 a.m. Saturday, approximately one mile north of Cold Creek Trail near Somersett.

Saturday's Red Flag Warning, which covered several counties in northwestern Nevada and northeastern California, ended at 11 p.m. last night.

The warning was issued due to windy, dry conditions throughout the region.

Sunday's forecast for the area of the Hawk Fire predicts sunny skies and patchy smoke, with light southwest winds reaching up to 10 mph in the afternoon. Highs are expected between 89 and 94. Partly cloudy conditions are expected Sunday night, with west winds up to 10 mph before decreasing overnight.

Partly cloudy conditions with southwest winds 10-15 mph are expected on Monday.

Evacuation centers for Hawk Fire

Shelters have been set up for those under evacuation orders. Those include:

Evacuation center: Reno-Sparks Convention Center, Hall 4, 4590 S. Virginia Street

Access the evacuation center from Kietzke Lane and enter through Door 20F.

Please do not bring pets to the evacuation center.

Small animal evacuations: Washoe County Regional Animal Services, 2825 Longley Lane

Large animal evacuations: Ironwood Event Center, 5600 Whiskey Springs Road

Turn right into the second driveway. Please check in at the main office.

Evelyn Mount Northeast Community Center is no longer an evacuation shelter for the Hawk Fire.

search_result.title: Reno man battles Bug wildfire as neighbors homes burn down
search_result.text:
Updated Aug. 12, 2026, 1:09 p.m. ET

With a shovel and a garden hose, Daniel Bartell has been fighting since just after midnight Sunday to save his 10-acre property, 45 animals and the home his wife loves in the North Valleys.

Bartell and his wife, Monique, were among the first Reno-area residents threatened by the Bug Fire, a fast-growing blaze that started Saturday afternoon near the Nevada-California state line and later merged with the Fred Mountain Fire farther to the east. The combined fires have destroyed homes, caused thousands to evacuate and burned more than 66,000 acres.

But the Bartells' home on Deerlodge Road in Reno is still standing. Some of their neighbors aren't so lucky.

"We were actually doing pretty good, and all of a sudden the winds flipped on us," Monique Bartell said of the fire's first day.

The merged fires became a serious threat when shifting winds pushed flames directly toward the couple's property, about 30 miles north of downtown Reno.

Three homes between the advancing fire and the Bartells' house were destroyed, Monique said. She believes additional homes in an area where she has about a dozen neighbors also were lost.

Fire officials have not released a count of homes destroyed or the full extent of the damage. Several residents near the Bartells have confirmed on social media that they lost their homes, including an engaged couple whose home was destroyed just weeks before their planned September wedding. A Reno real estate agent also posted that her home burned to the ground.

"The homes of the families that fled during the evacuations all burned," Monique said. "Our home and the home of a neighbor who stayed to fight the fire are still standing."

Fighting to save their home from wildfire

Daniel remained on the property as flames swept across the open desert. He borrowed water from a neighbor who has large water tanks.

"My husband could see the flames coming and hitting other homes first," sending up large black plumes of smoke as a structure caught fire, Monique said. "It gave him time to save our house."

The fire destroyed several sheds and burned much of the feed stored for the couple's animals. About half of their property is scorched, with blackened sagebrush ending just feet from their home.

The threat isn't over, either. On Tuesday night, new evacuation warnings and winds were again threatening their property.

Law enforcement blocks wife from returning to check on husband, animals

Monique said Wednesday morning that her husband stayed up again all night putting out hot spots on their property.

She's frustrated. She tried to go back Wednesday morning to check on her husband and animals and was stopped by law enforcement.

"I need to feed the animals and water them," she told the Reno Gazette Journal. She had loaded her truck with feed for her animals since what they had burned in the fire.

"I can't get to the animals to feed them," she said. "I'm frustrated and I'm tired and I'm out of options."

Their home was an animal sanctuary

The couple had been working to improve their piece of paradise, bought for $55,000 five years ago. They were planning on buying a mobile home to add to the yurt, 10,000-square-foot trailer and large deck they put on the land.

Monique, who works at Walmart, said it quickly became both an affordable dream property and a makeshift rescue for animals that found their way into her care.

Their animals include two emus, 17 goats, seven turkeys, peacocks, several pigs, homing pigeons and dogs.

As heartbreaking as it is, she said she is now searching for new homes or long-term foster placements for most of the animals.

"We just can't be sure they're safe here anymore," she said. "I can't protect them."

When evacuation warnings were issued, Monique left to stay with family in a nearby area not under evacuation, but Daniel refused to leave.

"He has not left," Monique said. "He was able to save all of our animals."

With only a small horse trailer, evacuating dozens of animals was never an option, she said. Despite repeated pleas from Monique to flee with her, Daniel stayed to fight the fire.

"I'm not leaving my house," he told her. "This is all I've got."

This story has been updated Wednesday morning.

search_result.title: Bug and Stallion fires evac orders in place, here's what to pack
search_result.text:
Aug. 10, 2026 Updated Aug. 11, 2026, 9:55 p.m. ET

The Bug Fire north of Reno and the Stallion Fire west of Pyramid Lake have burned tens of thousands of acres and prompted widespread evacuation orders.

Here's what Northern Nevadans can do to get ready before the evacuation order hits, from packing a go-bag to knowing what to do when wildfire approaches and everything in between.

Stay up to date on the latest evacuation news for the fires on rgj.com.

What to pack if you have to evacuate your home

The University of Nevada, Reno's Agriculture, Biotechnology and Natural Resources Extension has a peer-reviewed list of go-bag essentials for evacuations which includes:

Important documents such as insurance policies, medical records, birth certificates and banking info

ATM, credit and debit cards and cash in small bills

Medications, prescription (Rx) numbers and vaccination records (for people and pets)

Non-perishable food and bottled water for 72 hours

Driver’s license, passport and backup computer files or passwords

A home inventory (consider making a video inventory now, prior to an emergency)

Photographs of the exterior of the house and landscape

A printed address book with medical and veterinary contacts

Cell phone charger, car charger and battery packs

Toiletries and clothing for three to five days

Family heirlooms, photo albums and videos

Batteries

What should I wear during an evacuation?

If you’re ordered to evacuate due to wildfire, what you wear can reduce your risk of injury. The University of Nevada, Reno Extension recommends wearing only cotton or wool clothing — long pants, a long-sleeved shirt or jacket, a hat and boots — to help protect your skin from heat and embers.

The U.S. Department of Agriculture notes that natural fibers like cotton and wool char before they melt, unlike synthetic materials, which can melt onto skin and cause severe burns.

UNR's Extension recommends carrying gloves and goggles. It also recommends wearing a NIOSH N95 or P100 mask, which will help filter out particulates and protect your lungs.

How can I plan when I might need to evacuate?

Before a wildfire threatens your area, it’s important to create a full evacuation plan — not just for yourself, but for your family, pets and home. The Extension recommends starting with the basics: map out escape routes, choose a meeting point in case you’re separated, and assign someone outside the area to help relay information.

Once you’ve laid that groundwork, you’ll need to consider the next steps — how to evacuate animals, what to do if you don’t drive, how to prep your home before leaving and how to know when it’s safe to return. Here’s how to build out that full plan:

Evacuating your family and making a plan

Before a wildfire is near, it’s important to make a detailed evacuation plan with your family. UNR’s Extension has several recommendations:

Plan multiple evacuation routes from your home

Designate a safe meeting place for everyone to congregate if you get separated

Assign a trusted contact to relay your evacuation plans

Register for a local emergency notification system like Reverse 911 or CodeRed You can also register in Washoe County's emergency database and keep it updated



If a fire is burning nearby and evacuation is likely, try to evacuate children, seniors or anyone who may need additional time or assistance first.

Evacuating your pets, livestock and other animals

If you have large animals or livestock, the Extension recommends having a trailer and reliable vehicle ready. Practice loading animals into the trailer before an emergency arises to reduce stress and ensure safety.

All animals should have some form of identification, such as a collar or microchip. Keep veterinary records and medications in a sealable, easy-to-grab bag stored in a central location.

Additional tips include:

Pack food, water and bowls in easy-to-carry, sealed containers

Assign each pet to a specific family member as part of a buddy system

Coordinate with neighbors who can help if you’re not home

Identify friends or relatives who can house your animals if you’re displaced. "This can be especially helpful for livestock and poultry," UNR's Extension said.

Secure a crate for each animal, with only one per carrier. Even calm pets may panic and try to escape during emergencies

If you must leave animals behind, notify your local animal control or emergency services immediately so they can attempt a rescue

Prepare your transportation for an evacuation

If you don’t drive, arrange transportation in advance with friends, neighbors or a local service.

If you do drive, take steps to ensure a fast and safe evacuation:

Keep your vehicle's gas tank full

Roll up the windows on your vehicle

Place essential items in the car

Park facing out of your driveway or garage

If parking in a garage, disconnect the electric door opener and lift the door manually

Close the garage door when you leave

Prepare your home during an evacuation

Before you leave your home during an evacuation, UNR's Extension recommends:

Closing all interior doors

Leaving a light on in each room

Removing lightweight, non-fire-resistant curtains and other combustible materials from around windows

Close fire-resistant drapes, shutters, and blinds

Turn off all pilot lights

Move overstuffed furniture, such as couches and easy chairs, to the center of the room

Close fireplace damper

Close or block off any doggie-doors

Lock up firearms or valuables

Place combustible patio furniture and barbecues in the house, garage or awayfrom the home

Shut off propane at the tank or natural gas at the meter, and clear the area of combustible material

Close all exterior vents, doors, and windows

Leave gates unlocked

Turn on outside lights

If available and if there’s time, cover windows, attic openings, and vents with plywood at least half an inch thick

Ensure that all garden hoses are connected to faucets and turned off

Don’t leave sprinklers or water running; doing so can reduce water pressure for firefighters

Ensure that house numbers and street signs are visible and reflective if possible

search_result.text:
Updated Aug. 24, 2026, 2:00 p.m. ET

Crews struggled to contain a large wildfire near Reno, Nevada, that has forced thousands of people to flee their homes, destroyed structures and caused multiple injuries.

The Hawk Fire ignited Aug. 22 and quickly consumed more than 15,000 acres, or 23 square miles, near Reno as strong winds and dry brush fueled the flames, according to the National Interagency Fire Center. The blaze was 0% contained as of Monday, Aug. 24.

Officials ordered about 42,000 people to evacuate their homes, and another 40,000 were placed under evacuation warnings and urged to leave the area. Road closures were in effect across much of the area northwest of downtown Reno.

Nevada Gov. Joe Lombardo declared an emergency for Washoe County, which includes Reno and the northeast portion of Lake Tahoe. Local authorities opened temporary shelters, and the public school district for Washoe County canceled classes.

The fire has consumed an undetermined number of buildings, Shane Akerson, a battalion chief with the Truckee Meadows Fire Protection District, said at a briefing Aug. 23. The fire, which started in the Peavine Peak area of the Humboldt-Toiyabe National Forest, was human-caused, and the source of the ignition was under investigation.

At least six people had been injured, including three civilians and three first responders, Akerson said.

'A hard night': Residents describe frenzied evacuation

Thousands of people across northwest Reno received "Go Now" notifications Aug. 22 as strong winds spread the wildfire. Residents described idling in traffic as roads became jammed with evacuees.

For brothers Andrew Garcia and Logan Mann, fleeing with their grandmother from her apartment meant gathering three dogs and seven cats in a matter of minutes.

"We saw flames hitting our apartment and other homes burning," Andrew, 14, told The Reno Gazette-Journal, part of the USA TODAY Network.

Andrew said they left the apartment about 3 p.m. local time on Aug. 22 and spent the night at the Reno-Sparks Convention Center, where authorities had established a temporary shelter for evacuees.

Jenni Lejarza, along with her children and grandchildren, also spent the night at the convention center after trying to find a hotel room. After the fire broke out, they had monitored its spread and believed they were in the clear. But around 10 p.m. Aug. 22, they were ordered to leave.

"We had even unpacked all of our important documents and belongings, so when we got the alert to leave now, it was scary and fast," Lejarza said.

"It was OK, but a hard night."

Dry conditions, wind could further fuel Hawk Fire

More than 800 firefighters responded to the scene, along with hundreds of law enforcement personnel, Washoe County Sheriff Darin Balaam said. He added that members of the National Guard were being sent to the area.

The fire broke out as much of the western part of the United States was in drought, according to the U.S. Drought Monitor. Washoe County was suffering abnormally dry and moderate drought conditions as of Aug. 18, the monitor said.

According to the last update from fire officials, high winds and dry brush were expected to contribute to "increased fire activity."

"Over the next 12 hours, the fire is expected to continue to make moderate to high intensity runs in pockets of dense fuels," the fire center said Aug. 23.

The Hawk Fire was one of 200 new wildfires reported across the nation Aug. 22 as large wildfires were reported in 18 states, according to the the interagency fire center's daily situation report.

Contributing: Dinah Voyles Pulver

search_result.title: Bug Fire Tuesday: Parts of Palomino Valley told to 'evacuate now'
search_result.text:
Aug. 11, 2026 Updated Aug. 12, 2026, 8:42 a.m. ET

For updates on the Bug Fire and Stallion Fire on Wednesday, Aug. 12, click here.

Ongoing wildfires north of Reno-Sparks have burned more than 93,000 acres since Saturday, forcing thousands of residents to evacuate a wide area stretching from the Nevada-California State Line to the shores of Pyramid Lake.

The Bug Fire, first reported Saturday, had burned 61,803 acres as of 8 p.m. Tuesday. It has merged with the Fred Mountain Fire and stretched from U.S. 395 in California to Winnemucca Ranch Road in Nevada by Tuesday evening.

The Stallion Fire, a separate wildfire south of Pyramid Lake, has burned 31,548 acres since Monday.

The combined mandatory evacuation zone for the fires surpassed more than 500 square miles, with an additional 300 under evacuation warnings.

Although initial reports had the Bug Fire as high as 4% containment, both fires were listed at 0% containment as of 8 p.m. Tuesday.

Here's what we know as of Tuesday evening.

Nine schools to be closed Wednesday due to Bug, Stallion fires

The Washoe County School District on Tuesday evening announced Wednesday closures for nine schools in the area of ongoing wildfires. Those schools are:

Alyce Taylor Elementary School

Desert Heights Elementary School

Jesse Hall Elementary School

Lemmon Valley Elementary School

Natchez Elementary School

Silver Lake Elementary School

Spanish Springs Elementary School

Shaw Middle School

Spanish Springs High School

Natchez Elementary was in session on Monday, but classes there were canceled for Tuesday. All eight other schools on the list have yet to hold classes during the first week of the 2026-27 WCSD school year due to nearby wildfires.

Evacuation order issued for Warm Springs area of Palomino Valley and by Pyramid Lake

New evacuations are in effect on the east side of Pyramid Highway north of Iron Wood in Palomino Valley.

A robocall to area residents advised, "This is Washoe County Emergency Management. Wildfire in the Warm Springs portion of Palomino Valley. Evacuate now. Watch for first responders."

Evacuees must utilize southbound SR 445 (Pyramid Highway) to evacuate the area. SR 446 is closed in both directions at the junction and is impassable due to the Stallion Fire.

Gusty winds are making firefighting efforts difficult and containment is at 0%. The Washoe County Sheriff's Office posted that a dozer line Tuesday night is expected to make progress as overnight temperatures drop.

For the most current evacuation zones, road closures and incident updates, please monitor Perimeter Map.The Washoe County Sheriff's Office reminds residents to use caution in and around the area, remain alert for changing conditions and be aware of emergency vehicles and personnel responding to the incident.

In addition to the Bug Fire evacuations, additional evacuation warning areas have been added to the southeast and northwest side of the Stallion Fire burning next to Pyramid Lake.

The two fires have burned a combined 91,000 acres according to perimetermap.

Evacuation center remains available at Evelyn Mount Community Center

The Washoe County Human Services Agency posted that it and American Red Cross of Nevada are ready to receive evacuees at the Evelyn Mount Community Center, 1301 Valley Road, Reno. They have beds, pillows, blankets, water, food and games.

Discounted hotel rooms are also available in the area for those needing to evacuate. This link offers a complete list: https://www.emergencywashoe.com/updates/

Woman arrested on arson charge, accused of starting Fred Mountain Fire

A woman was arrested for allegedly starting the Fred Mountain Fire on Sunday, the Washoe County Sheriff's Office said in a Facebook post Tuesday.

According to the investigation, Christine Mitchell, 47, left a residence near 1300 block of Freds Mountain Road and intentionally started multiple fires in the area, resulting in what became known as the Fred Mountain Fire.

Her bail is set at $80,000.

As fire personnel responded to the Fred Mountain Fire shortly after it began, Mitchell flagged down responding crews and told them she had intentionally started the fire. Fire personnel then transferred Mitchell into the custody of the Washoe County Sheriff’s Office.

Washoe County Sheriff’s Office deputies and detectives developed probable cause to arrest Mitchell on charges of third degree arson and possession of a controlled substance of less than 14 grams.

“I am proud of the work our deputies and detectives put into this investigation and thankful for the coordination with our fire service partners. Starting another fire while crews were already committed to an active wildfire placed additional strain on emergency resources and unnecessarily threatened additional portions of our community. We will continue to thoroughly investigate this incident and hold the individual responsible accountable,” said Sheriff Darin Balaam.

The Washoe County Sheriff’s Office encourages anyone with information related to this incident, or who may have observed suspicious activity associated with the Fred Mountain Fire, to contact law enforcement.

This remains an ongoing investigation, and additional charges may be forthcoming as investigators continue reviewing the circumstances surrounding the incident.

4:30 p.m. Tuesday update:

The Bug Fire has grown to more than 57,000 over three days, followed by the Stallion Fire which grew from 25 acres to more than 22,000 acres in 24 hours.

The Bug Fire has claimed structures, but officials could not say how many homes are lost or damaged. However, no injuries have been reported to date, Southwest Area Incident Management's Commander Caleb Finch said at a news conference Tuesday afternoon.

Both fires continue to expand and grow every hour, and Finch said the fire efforts are being led by a joint operation of multiple agencies as of Tuesday afternoon, including federal support, out-of-state agencies and other local firefighters.

Washoe County Sheriff Darin Balaam said more than 4,000 families are displaced as a result of the evacuation orders. Officials are unsure how many total homes are currently threatened.

Finch said the incident is dynamic, and the firefighters are focused on getting people out and protecting the homes, so they may not have informed residents if their homes were lost yet.

"No doubt we got some tough days ahead of us with these winds and the challenging conditions," Finch said.

Operations chief Jayson Coil said the method right now is a large-scale protection, which means protecting subdivisions and neighborhoods as a whole instead of individual structures. Even if the fire is adjacent to neighborhoods, their priority is preventing the fire from impacting more homes.

"We like to get a place to start with that fire and move forward, but we haven't been able to do that. There's been too many communities threatened simultaneously and on different sides of the fire," Coil said.

"That fight is going on all the way around the fire today and is likely to be going on for several days to come."

Finch also said the team is giving their full effort to not let the Bug Fire merge with the Stallion Fire after the Fred Mountain fire was absorbed by the Bug Fire.

"But we got to let the conditions change. We will work hard to make sure that doesn't happen," Finch said. "I think we can get enough resources to make a difference in this fire ... They are sending us everything they have."

Finch said residents should monitor peimtermap.com to see if their homes are in an evacuation zone since the fire is fast-moving.

The Bug, Fred Mountain, Stallion Fire Facebook page has all the newest information on power, evacuations, emergency needs and more.

More than 1,000 still without power after NV Energy lines de-energized due to fire threat

More than 1,000 NV Energy customers are still without power after the utility implemented emergency de-energizations as wildfires continue to burn near power equipment.

NV Energy said Tuesday that it had restored power to about 700 customers who were affected by wildfire activity in the area, but 1,076 remain without electricity.

NV Energy proactively cuts power in areas at risk from wildfires to reduce the risk of electric equipment causing secondary ignitions.

Areas affected by de-energizations include Red Rock, Antelope Valley, Palomino Valley and Nixon. All customers impacted by the temporary shutdowns are in locations that are under evacuation orders or warnings, according to NV Energy.

NV Energy has not provided a timeline for when power will be restored to affected customers.

With the fire still active, the utility is working with fire officials to determine when it will be safe to restore power.

“NV Energy understands that the lack of a timeline is frustrating and recognizes the challenges extended outages create for customers and communities,” it said in a statement.

“To avoid providing inaccurate information or setting expectations that may change as conditions evolve, estimated restoration times have been temporarily removed.”

“Power cannot be restored until fire conditions improve,” NV Energy added.

Although safely restoring power remains the top priority for NV Energy, the company is advising affected customers to be prepared for a prolonged outage.

For more details, including information about the outage and resources for preparedness , the utility company recommends visiting its official site at nvenergy.com.

Bug Fire evacuation orders expanded to the east

3:25 p.m. Tuesday update: "Go Now" evacuation orders are now in place for Palomino Valley neighborhoods between Winnemucca Ranch Road and Nevada State Route 445 below Range Land Road.

The Bug Fire is now at 57,363 acres burned with 4% containment, and the Stallion Fire is at 22,428 with no containment listed as of the most recent updates.

Approximately 250 square miles are under evacuation orders due to the Bug and Stallion fires, with an additional 400 square miles under evacuation warnings.

3 p.m. Tuesday update: Southwest Complex Incident Management Team 1 is holding a press conference to provide updates on the battle against the Bug, Fred Mountain and Stallion fires.

The Bug and Fred Mountain fires have merged into a 44,304-acre fire, and the Stallion Fire increased overnight to 22,428 acres. The two wildfires have prompted evacuations and warnings from the Nevada-California state line to Nixon and Wadsworth east of Reno-Sparks.

Communities near the fires remain threatened by potential fire growth, BLM said. Evacuation recommendations are made by fire managers based on current and expected fire behavior, and evacuation warnings and orders are implemented by the Washoe County Sheriff’s Office.

Residents should rely on perimetermap.com for the most current evacuation information, including changes to evacuation status and repopulation.

Evacuation warning areas expand rapidly for Stallion Fire

New evacuation warnings have been issued for the Nixon area north of Sutcliffe Highway. Residents should be prepared to evacuate.

The Stallion Fire has burned 22,477 acres with 0% containment.

Evacuation zones for the wildfires covered an area of approximately 250 square miles as of 2 p.m. Tuesday.

California strike team arrives to help fight fire in Spanish Springs

Additional resources from Cal Fire, the Sonoma-Lake-Napa Unit, have deployed to Spanish Springs, the north Sparks community. The strike team consists of five engines and a battalion chief.

Spanish Springs is under an evacuation warning from Eagle Canyon Drive on the west side of Pyramid Highway. See Perimetermap.com for the current evacuation areas.

How Bug Fire, Fred Mountain Fire and Stallion Fire got their names

As with nearly all wildfires, the blazes burning north of Reno received names based on their starting locations.

Bug Fire: The fire started Saturday, Aug. 8 just over the Nevada-California state line near the California Agricultural Inspection Station – Long Valley on U.S. 395 south of Hallelujah Junction. The stations often are colloquially referred to as “bug stations” because inspectors look for invasive pests that could be harmful to California’s agricultural industry.

Fred Mountain Fire: Now merged with the larger Bug Fire, Fred Mountain Fire is a slight misnomer of its starting location on Freds Mountain. The fire was initially reported shortly before noon on Sunday, Aug. 9. The location originally was known as Fred’s Mountain, a name that dates back at least to 1901; it was the site of gold, silver, copper and lead mining in the early 20th century.

Stallion Fire: Burning since Monday morning, the Stallion Fire was named for its starting location near Stallion Drive, a road south of Pyramid Lake and east of Nixon near Moses Rock.

Evacuation 'go now' issued to parts of Spanish Springs, Nixon

11:55 a.m. Tuesday update: The "Go Now" evacuation zone has been extended to parts of Spanish Springs along north Eagle Canyon Road and Loop Road; and the "Get Set To Evacuate" zone for the Bug Fire has been extended to neighborhoods west of Pyramid Way and north of Eagle Canyon Drive near Spanish Springs High School.

New evacuation warnings have been issued for the Nixon area north of Nevada State Route 446 due to the nearby Stallion Fire. The highway extends from Nixon along the southwest shore of Pyramid Lake to Nevada State Route 445, aka Pyramid Way.

Residents should rely on perimetermap.com for the most current evacuation information, including changes to evacuation status and repopulation.

The evacuation center at Evelyn Mount Community Center, 1013 Valley Road, Reno, remains the official evacuation center. Washoe County Regional Animal Services is accepting small animals at 2825 Longley Lane. The large-animal shelter at the Reno-Sparks Livestock Events Center currently has more than 150 animals. Space and resources are limited, and residents who are able are encouraged to self-evacuate animals to a friend or family member’s home.

The Bug Fire remained at 4% containment as of 11:30 a.m. Tuesday. Current firefighting efforts are focused on protecting communities, transit corridors and utility infrastructure, the National Interagency Fire Center reported.

Bug, Fred Mountain, Stallion firefighting efforts challenged by hot, windy conditions Tuesday afternoon

11:20 a.m. Tuesday update:

Dry fuel and hot, windy conditions could hamper efforts to fight the Bug, Fred Mountain and Stallion fires Tuesday afternoon.

The National Weather Service predicts a chance of showers and thunderstorms in northwestern Nevada this afternoon, with possible gusts of 45-55 mph. The NWS also warned of possible flash flooding as storms move in Wednesday and Thursday.

What started the Bug, Fred and Stallion fires? 'Human caused' can mean many things

Fire officials say the three fires burning in Northern Nevada were human-caused, meaning they were not started by a natural event such as lightning.

The Bug, Fred Mountain and Stallion fires have burned 65,000 acres combined as of Tuesday, bolstered by strong winds and low humidity.

Officials have not identified the specific causes of the fires, but said each started independently and was not ignited by embers spreading from another blaze.

Asked about the possibility of them being intentionally set, fire officials said during a press conference Monday that nothing has been confirmed but all three starts will be investigated.

"The investigations are ongoing, so details are not available at this time," said Joe Shum, division chief with the Truckee Meadows Fire Protection District.

According to the National Park Service, about 85% of wildfires in the United States are caused by people.

Fire officials said it takes only a small spark to ignite the type of fast-moving wildfires seen in Northern Nevada.

Common causes of human-caused wildfires include:

Dragging tire chains

Hot exhaust pipes

Worn brakes

Blown tires

Catalytic converters parked over dry grass

Lawn mowers

Industrial tools

Unattended or escaped campfires

Off-road vehicles, including ATVs and motorcycles

Cooking devices

Open burning

Power lines

Railroad operations

Discarded smoking materials

Fireworks

Target shooting

Arson

Original story:

The evacuation warning and order areas for the Bug, Fred Mountain and Stallion fires merged overnight Monday and now stretch from the Nevada-California state line to the southwest of Pyramid Lake.

The Bug Fire has burned 16,680 acres and is 3% contained, the Bureau of Land Management reported Monday night.

The Fred Mountain Fire, burning about 9 miles north of Lemmon Valley, is 3,482 acres and 0% contained.

The Stallion Fire southeast of Pyramid Lake is over 20,000 acres and 0% containment.

The fires remain active, with wind-driven runs, flanking and short-range spotting, BLM said. Critically dry fuels, hot and dry conditions, and afternoon winds continue to support rapid fire spread and extended burning periods.

Crews are continuing fireline construction on the north, east and south sides of the Bug Fire, while structure protection resources assess and protect threatened structures and establish defensible space where conditions allow, BLM posted.

search_result.title: Bug Fire Friday update: 'A light at the end of the tunnel'
search_result.text:
Updated Aug. 14, 2026, 8:22 p.m. ET

The Bug and Stallion fires north of Reno-Sparks have burned more than 130,000 acres since Saturday, forcing thousands of residents to evacuate a wide area from northeastern California to Pyramid Lake.

But firefighters have made significant progress, thanks to an increase in available personnel and an assist from afternoon rainstorms Wednesday and Thursday.

The Bug Fire, which has burned through 91,125 acres, saw containment more than double to 31%, according to Caleb Finch, incident commander with the Southwest Area Incident Management Team 1. Containment for the Stallion Fire, which has burned 40,698 acres, was at 44%.

“Crews secured the northwest flank of the Bug Fire, allowing Highway 395 to reopen, and evacuation orders have been lifted for portions of Red Rock Road and Hungry Valley, allowing those residents to return home,” Finch said in a statement early Friday.

“As crews continue to strengthen and secure containment lines, we are working closely with the Washoe County Sheriff’s Office and Tribal authorities to reduce evacuation levels in additional communities as soon as conditions allow.”

A total of 23 crews and 771 fire personnel are attacking the wildfires — 579 on the Bug Fire and 192 on the Stallion Fire. A total of 66 engines, eight helicopters and 24 dozers have been deployed between the two blazes.

Residents should rely on perimetermap.com and watchduty.org for the most current evacuation information, including changes to evacuation status and repopulation.

Cooler temperatures and the possibility of more rain are in the forecast Friday. Sunny skies in the morning will give way to partially cloudy conditions with a slight chance of showers and thunderstorms in the afternoon; highs in the area will be 66 to 76. Conditions will be mostly clear overnight with a slight chance of showers and thunderstorms in the evening. Lows are expected to be 37 to 47.

Weather remains a wild card that can help or hinder firefighting efforts.

“Thunderstorms with the potential for rain are forecasted again today, with cooler temperatures and higher humidity moderating fire behavior (but) gusty and erratic thunderstorm outflow winds up to 40 mph remain possible and can push fire in new directions with little warning,” Finch said.

“A warming and drying trend is forecast in the coming days, which is why crews are working aggressively now to secure (lines) while conditions are favorable.”

Smoke from various wildfires in the region, and other regional fires may also ontinue to impact the surrounding communities, Finch added.

Here's what we know about the fires on Friday, Aug. 14.

'A light at the end of the tunnel'

Joseph Colacurcio, a captain for the Washoe County Sheriff's Office, said roughly 2,600 evacuees are still displaced from the Bug and Stallion fires.

However, many areas have reopened and moved from a red "evacuate now" zone to a yellow "get ready" zone, or to a blue cleared zone.

Areas that will be repopulated include Palomino Valley areas, including Highway 445 to the east and 445 to the west of Winnemucca Ranch Road and the Antelope Valley area. Roughly 282 individuals will stay evacuated.

The same nine structures reported lost Thursday are the only ones still reported Friday, the sheriff's office said.

The following road closures will remain in place:

Red Rock Road / Bird Springs Road

Stead Airport at Alpha Avenue / Mount Anderson Street

Red Rock Road / Clydesdale Drive

New road closure locations are also in effect, restricting access into the Rancho Haven community:

Winnemucca Ranch Road, prior to the Moon Rocks turnoff

Antelope Valley Road, where the roadway transitions to dirt north of Goldwood Road

All other previously established road closures not listed above have been lifted.

Despite the ongoing fire, TMFPD Deputy Fire Chief Shannon Lewis said the morale of the firefighters is getting better.

Colacurcio said a lot of enforcement are doing an emergency routine, including many working 12- to 16- hour shifts.

"I believe morale is increasing after a few tough days," Colacurcio said.

Lewis said they've had firefighter crews working since the beginning of the fire, and have had rest breaks, but many are working tirelessly to protect the community.

"I think we're starting to see the light at the end of the tunnel," Lewis said.

NV Energy reports almost full restoration

All customers power has been restored from the Bug and Stallion Fires, except for roughly 20 residents east of the Palomino Valley area, on a road going up to Virginia Peak.

Senior Vice President of NV Energy Jesse Murray said those customers power is also expected to be restored today.

"These outages are definitely disruptive, we know that. Very impactful. But we feel that emergency de-energization is an important tool that helps us reduce wildfire risk during these active fire incidents," Murray said.

Nine WCSD schools will remain closed Friday

The Washoe County School District announced Friday, Aug. 14 closures for nine schools in the area of ongoing wildfires. Those schools are:

Jesse Hall Elementary School

Desert Heights Elementary School

Lemmon Valley Elementary School

Natchez Elementary School

Silver Lake Elementary School

Spanish Springs Elementary School

Alyce Taylor Elementary School

Shaw Middle School

Spanish Springs High School

Natchez Elementary was in session Monday, but classes there were canceled for Tuesday. The eight other schools have yet to hold classes during the first week of the 2026-27 WCSD school year due to the wildfires.

New evacuation map shows lifted areas near Silver Lake

Evacuation orders have been reduced to evacuation warnings in the Red Rock Road and Hungry Valley areas.

The following road and access changes are also now in effect:

Hungry Valley: The road closure in Hungry Valley will be moved to Eagle Canyon Drive and Calle de la Plata, reopening limited access up to that location.

Red Rock: The road closure at Red Rock Road and Adobe Drive will be moved north to Red Rock Road and Bird Springs Road, reopening limited access between Adobe Drive and Bird Springs Road.

Lemmon Valley: The road closure at Ramsey Way and Lemmon Drive will be moved to Antelope Valley Road and Freds Mountain Road, reopening limited access up to that location.

The Washoe County Sheriff's Office said in a Facebook post that residents returning to these areas should use caution, remain alert for emergency vehicles and personnel, and continue looking for additional changes.

9 homes lost, 3,000 residents still displaced

Nine homes have been announced lost in the Bug Fire, officials announced Thursday. It was the first confirmation on a number of structures lost during the wildfire.

"We've had communication with everyone who's lost their home," TMFPD Chief Richard Edwards told media.

The homes were primarily around the Red Rock area.

All of the homeowners will also have the chance to get back to their properties without having to contend with the other residents trying to get back into their homes at the same time.

Lassen County Sheriff’s Office also confirmed Thursday two civilians who sustained burn injuries from the Bug Fire were transported by care flight to the UC Davis Burn Center for treatment.

The circumstances around how the injuries happened is preliminary, and no information about the individuals can be released currently.

Southwest Area Incident Commander Jason Coil said there’s been no firefighter injuries and no fatalities reported.

Three thousand residents remain displaced from their homes during the evacuations.

Washoe County Sheriff Darin Balaam told residents to keep watch on the evacuation zones on perimetermap.com, since the agencies are reassessing where they can repopulate areas every 12 hours.

Balaam said law enforcement will still be present even as areas are open so they can monitor the areas and prevent looters.

Evacuees can also enter the red zones, if it’s safe, as long as they give their driver’s license or identification cards. Many are being let in to feed their livestock or grab medications.

The Bug Fire and Stallion Fire are still under investigation. One arrest has been made on the Fred Mountain Fire.

Fire behavior improved, containment lines holding

Southwest Area Incident Commander Jason Coil said they have a line around many parts of the fire helping to contain it from growing, whether it’s roads or a dozer line they put in.

“You can expect to see the containment growing rapidly today and then moving forward,” Coil said.

The biggest areas of concern are keeping the containment lines cold, and checking to make sure the burnt out portions with no containment lines are cold — which firefighters do by feeling with their bare hand to make sure there’s no heat.

Crews also delivered good news regarding the Dogskin Mountains, which has been one of the areas of concern in recent days.

“In the Dogskin Mountains, we had a really good day yesterday,” said Southwest Area Team One Operation Section Chief Ashleigh D’Antonio on Friday morning. “We’re looking to lock off this piece of ground … within the next couple of shifts.”

Firefighter schedules are long, with camp at Rancho San Rafael

The TMFPD fire chief said the firefighters are out on the line roughly 12 to 14-hours a day, and can work up to 21 days, depending on what agency they’re from and the what they are needed for, before their mandatory break.

When they come back to the camp at Rancho San Rafael Regional Park, they have all the resources they need including sleeping areas, catered food, showering facilities and laundry facilities.

“It’s a small city really,” Edwards said.

Rain helps contain portions of wildfires; winds push Bug Fire westward

Fire crews reported significant progress on some parts of the Bug and Stallion Fires as rainy weather and increased humidity helped firefighting efforts.

“Yesterday, wetting rains over the fire area aided crews who were directly attacking the fire’s edge, protecting structures, and securing properties in communities around both fires,” Finch said.

Fire crews made “strong progress” on the southern flank at Cold Springs and the northern flank at the Petersen Mountains for the Bug Fire.

Crews also secured more areas on the eastern flank toward Palomino Valley for the Stallion Fire.

Resources and manpower have been strained for crews working on the Bug and Stallion Fires as high fire activity across the West limited assistance available to fight both wildfires.

Drier conditions are also expected to return over the weekend, which could lead to more challenging conditions for fire crews.

“Over the coming days, the primary operational priority will be capturing and securing perimeters of the Bug Fire and the Stallion Fire,” Finch said.

“Ground personnel are focused on securing lines near the fire’s edge, prioritizing structure protection for residences in the area and safety for the firefighters and the public.”

Thunderstorms to bring rain, cooler temperatures to Reno area

Rain continues to be in the forecast for today for the greater Reno area, providing potential relief for crews battling multiple wildfires.

The National Weather Service is forecasting a 20% chance of showers from 2 to 8 p.m., Friday, which brings not only moisture but cooler weather as well.

The forecast, however, also includes a chance for thunderstorms, which can potentially spark new fires.

Washoe County works on repopulation plan for Silver Knolls evacuees

Washoe County Sheriff Darin Balaam said they are currently repopulating the Silver Knolls neighborhood to the beginning of Red Rock, and expect to allow more evacuees into the area based on which areas they believe are safe from fire danger.

Balaam detailed the plans at a community meeting at the O'Brien Middle School on Wednesday evening.

"Bear with us as we make sure when we allow you in there, we don't have to go back in and get you out because the fire changed directions," Balaam said.

Truckee Meadows Fire Protection District’s Fire Chief Richard Edwards said this process will continue through Thursday.

“Tonight you will probably see some map changes, and some of those evacuations downgraded in the next 12 hours,” Edwards said.

As for the weather, the rain that came in Wednesday afternoon through the evening was a "pleasant surprise," according to the Stewart Turner, the fire behavior analyst.

"It did help on the fire, but you got to remember not everywhere recieved the rain we saw," Turner said. "We're going to have a better chance of rain for both fires tomorrow."

The east side of Reno saw heavy rain, but Turner said the Stallion Fire was the only fire that got rain. The north part of the Stallion Fire got 0.4 inches of rain, and the south side got 0.25 inches of rain.

However, the team is projecting a quarter of an inch of rain on the Bug and Stallion fires on Thursday, as well as more moisture throughout the week.

D'Antonio also said there was lightning that struck Wednesday evening, and started a small fire near the Stallion Fire, but the firefighters put it out quickly.

"That threat is real," D'Antonio said.

As for the fire behavior, the Bug Fire shifted west back towards the Nevada State Line Wednesday by high winds. This is why officials closed U.S. 395 in both directions at the Nevada state line to Doyle, California in the evening.

The Bug Fire is projected to grow northeast toward the Dogskin Mountains, and continue west towards the Nevada-California border. Turner said the south end of the Bug Fire has been burning out, specifically in the Red Rock area and neighborhoods of Lemmon Valley, and they don't expect to see more fire growth in those areas.

The Stallion Fire is projected to stabilize a bit over the next few days due to the extra moisture, but it will push back towards the southwest after the moisture dries out.

"Things are changing as we speak," D'Antonio said.
