Updated Aug. 10, 2026, 11:43 p.m. ET

8:30 p.m. Monday update:

Evacuation warnings have been issued for parts of Nixon, east of the Stallion Fire that has burned 1,000 acres.

The Stallion Fire began at 8:45 a.m. Monday southwest of Pyramid Lake. That and the Fred Mountain fire and Bug Fire north of Reno have been determined to be human-caused, officials said Monday, but no further information was released due to ongoing investigations.

8:15 p.m. Monday update:

The Washoe County School District announced Monday night it would again shut down schools amid the threat of wildfires.

The district said the Bug Fire continues to impact the community including with evacuations and power outages. The district said that in consultation with fire officials, eight schools would remained closed a second day.

The schools closed on Tuesday, Aug. 11

Jesse Hall Elementary School

Spanish Springs Elementary School

Desert Heights Elementary School

Silver Lake Elementary School

Lemmon Valley Elementary School

Shaw Middle School

Spanish Springs High School

Alyce Taylor Elementary School

The district also said it will not provide bus transportation in areas designated red or yellow, meaning they are areas evacuated or under watch for evacuation.

4:55 p.m. Monday update:

Nevada Gov. Lombardo has declared a state of emergency for areas of Washoe County and the Reno-Sparks Indian Colony impacted by ongoing wildfires.

“Thousands of Nevadans have been forced from their homes as these fires continue to threaten communities across Washoe County and the Reno-Sparks Indian Colony,” said Governor Joe Lombardo. “The state is taking every available step to support local responders, protect lives and property, and ensure the resources necessary to confront these fires are where they are needed most."

The declaration allows agencies across jurisdictions throughout the state to more rapidly provide assistance with northwestern Nevada's wildfire-fighting efforts. Lombardo also requested federal resources, including National Guard personnel and equipment.

Nevada Gov. Joe Lombardo, Washoe County Sheriff Darin Balaam, Reno-Sparks Indian Colony Chair Doug Gardipe and fire officials held a press conference Monday afternoon to recap firefighting efforts so far. Among the details:

The Bug Fire began around 3:30 p.m. Saturday near the California Agricultural Inspection Station - Long Valley.

The Fred Mountain Fire began around 10:45 a.m. Sunday on Fred's Mountain, Nevada.

The Stallion Fire began at 8:45 a.m. Monday southwest of Pyramid Lake, Nevada.

Approximately 350 personnel have been fighting the fire.

Investigators have determined all three fires to be human-caused, but no further information was released due to ongoing investigations.

A total of 10,000 people have been evacuated during the wildfires, although 4,000 have been allowed to return to the Cold Springs area.

One firefighter and one civilian have been injured and released.

Homes have been lost, but no further details were provided during the press briefing.

"We are always worried about the weather," said Truckee Meadows Fire Protection District Chief Richard Edwards. He noted they're keeping an eye on thunderstorms moving into the area — especially wind and lightning, which may exacerbate the fires; and rain, which could assist fire suppression.

TMFPD spokesperson Kimberly Flores said that each of the fire is named after a geographic location, like a street, mountain or structure. The Bug Fire for example was named after the agricultural inspection center in the area it started, also known as the "bug station."

4:15 p.m. Monday update: State and local officials are providing an update on the Bug, Fred Mountain and Stallion fires, all of which have been determined to be human-caused.

3:45 p.m. Monday update: The mandatory evacuation zone for the Bug Fire and Fred Mountain Fire has expanded to the north side of the Rancho Haven area, with evacuation warning areas expanding up toward Wildcat Hill and Dry Valley Creek.

The Bug Fire now stands at 16,680 acres burned, and remains at 4% containment. The Fred Mountain Fire is now at 3,482 acres, with no containment listed. The Stallion Fire remains at 1,000 acres, no containment listed.

View the latest evacuation maps at perimetermap.com/washoe.

3:10 p.m. Monday update: The size of the Stallion Fire has jumped to 1,000 acres, according to WildCAD, the dispatch system for wildland fire agencies.

Meanwhile, mandatory evacuation zones for the Bug Fire have expanded to the area north of the fire up to Shetland Circle between Red Rock Road and the Nevada-California state line.

The Stallion Fire, burning south of Pyramid Lake, is now the third fire north of Reno larger than 1,000 acres. No containment for the Stallion Fire has been announced.

The Bug Fire, which ignited on Saturday afternoon, is listed at 17,000 acres with 4% containment. The Fred Mountain Fire was last reported at 1,393 acres; it also has no announced containment percentage.

3:05 p.m. Monday update: Churchill County is offering dry camping facilities and covered horse stalls at no charge for those evacuating local wildfires.

The facilities are at the county's 3C Event Complex in Fallon, and are accessible at Miners Road off Sheckler Road.

Water is available, but evacuees will need to provide their own feed for livestock.

2:45 p.m. Monday update: Gov. Joe Lombardo and emergency officials will participate in a press conference at 4:30 p.m. Monday to provide updates on the Bug and Fred Mountain fires.

The press conference will take place at the Incident Command Post near the Reno-Stead Airport.

2:30 p.m. Monday update:

Evacuation warning areas for the Bug Fire have spread to the north of the fire, to the area west of Red Rock Road and east of the Nevada-California state line.

The Pyramid Lake Paiute Tribe has closed the lake to all boating and watercraft activities, and has authorized firefighting aircraft to dip into the lake to help fight the wildfire. The Tribe also has banned drone usage in the area.

"We cannot express enough thanks to the firefighting personnel," Pyramid Lake Paiute Tribe Chairman Steve Wadsworth wrote. "We pray for their safe return as well as the health and safety of our neighbors."

1:30 p.m. Monday update:

The Bug Fire and Fred Mountain Fire together have burned more than 18,000 acres of land in north Reno.

The Bug Fire has grown to an estimated 17,000 acres burned as of Tuesday afternoon. It has been determined to be human-caused, according to a news release from the Nevada State Office of the Bureau of Land Management.

The BLM said 300 resources are assigned to the Bug Fire and it is currently 4% contained.

Approximately 5,500 people have been evacuated, and the BLM says communities near the fire remain threatened by potential fire growth since the Bug Fire is wind-driven and is spreading rapidly due to hot and dry conditions.

“Rapid fire growth toward the east and Red Rock Road remains a concern,” the news release said.

Residents can evacuate at the official shelter at Evelyn Mount Community Center, located at 1301 Valley Road in Reno.

Small animals can be taken in at the Washoe County Regional Animal Services shelter, located at 2825 Longley Lane. Large animals are still being accepted at the Reno-Sparks Livestock Events Center at 1350 N Wells Ave. in Reno.

Animal Services Program Coordinator Quinn Sweet said as of Monday morning, there are 325 animals being kept at the livestock center, the majority being horses, but there is still space for more evacuated livestock.

However, the staffing and resources are limited, so residents in the red evacuation zones are being prioritized. Officials recommend evacuation of livestock to other locations if residents are able.

1 p.m. Monday update: The Ironwood Fire, a wildfire that burned 36 acres off the Pyramid Highway, was declared 100% contained shortly before 1 p.m. Monday.

Fire crews continue to battle the Bug Fire, Fred Mountain Fire, Stallion Fire and Hunter Fire around Reno. Evacuation zones and warning areas remain in place north of Reno due to the Bug Fire and Fred Mountain Fire.

Shannon Lewis, deputy chief of operations with the Truckee Meadows Fire Protection District, told media at midday Sunday that the Ironwood Fire was largely under control, but that crews were "mopping up" the blaze.

11 a.m. Monday update: The vegetation fire near Pyramid Lake has been named the Stallion Fire, currently listed as 25 acres.

The fire is about 16 miles east of the Fred Mountain Fire and about 2 1/2 miles from Pyramid Lake. It's the fourth named fire to the north of Reno since Saturday, following the Bug Fire (15,000 acres, according to the most recently available estimates), Fred Mountain Fire (1,393 acres) and Ironwood Fire (36 acres).

The Hunter Fire, another fire near Hunter Creek Trail west of Reno, is listed at 7.6 acres. The fire, first reported Friday evening, is listed at 10% containment. No structures were reported threatened as of 11 a.m. Monday.

10:45 a.m. Monday update: The Federal Emergency Management Agency on Monday morning granted the use of federal funds to fight the Bug Fire, which has been burning since midday Saturday.

FEMA Region 9 approved the Fire Management Assistant Grant, which will provide funding of up to 75% of the state's expenditures for firefighting efforts, including expenses for field camps, equipment use, materials, supplies, and mobilization and demobilization activities.

There were 220 personnel fighting the wildfire as of late Monday morning.

10 a.m. Monday update: The Reno-Stead Airport has closed to general aviation, but remains open for firefighting and military aircraft, the Reno-Tahoe Airport Authority announced Monday morning.

The airport is within the evacuation warning area for the Bug Fire and Fred Mountain Fire.

Reno-Tahoe International Airport, the region's primary commercial airport, remains unaffected.

Meanwhile, ground-based fire crews are working on an unnamed vegetation fire about 16 miles east of the Fred Mountain Fire and about 2 1/2 miles from Pyramid Lake.

Original story: The Bug Fire and Fred Mountain Fire burned more than 16,000 acres north of Reno over the weekend and into Monday as local, state and federal fire personnel battled to keep the blaze from nearby communities.

As of 8 a.m. Monday, the larger Bug Fire had consumed an estimated 15,000 acres. The Fred Mountain Fire to the east was listed at 1,393 acres with no containment estimate.

The Washoe County School District canceled what would have been the first day of the 2026-27 school year for about 6,000 students at eight campuses near the fire. The schools closed are:

Jesse Hall Elementary School

Spanish Springs Elementary School

Desert Heights Elementary School

Silver Lake Elementary School

Lemmon Valley Elementary School

Shaw Middle School

Spanish Springs High School

Alyce Taylor Elementary School

Evacuation orders remained in effect for areas of Lemmon, Golden and Hungry valleys to the north of Reno. Evacuation orders for most of Cold Springs were lifted Sunday evening. For the latest evacuation maps, visit perimetermap.com/washoe.

Evacuation shelters for the fire include:

Evelyn Mount Community Center, 1301 Valley Rd.

Nevada State Fairgrounds (also known as the Reno-Sparks Livestock Events Center), 1350 N. Wells Ave. (large animal shelter)

Power was out for thousands of customers within the affected area Sunday, but NV Energy had restored service to nearly all by early Monday morning.

Thunderstorms in northwestern Nevada likely later this week

No cause has been identified for any of the three fires north of Reno, but thunderstorms predicted for the region later this week are expected to heighten fire danger.

"Dangerous heat will intensify across the Desert Southwest and Intermountain West," the National Weather Service reported. "Hot, dry weather and increasing winds will allow elevated wildfire conditions to return to the northern Intermountain West, where air quality issues persist from ongoing fires."

The latest forecast for northwestern Nevada predicts a chance of thunderstorms between Tuesday and Saturday.

Monday: Sunny with patchy smoke in the morning, then partly cloudy in the afternoon; breezy with gusts of up to 30 mph at higher elevations. Highs 96-101 in the valleys and 80-90 at higher elevations. Clear with patchy smoke overnight; breezy with gusts of up to 30 mph at higher elevations. Lows 60-70 in the valleys and 49-59 at higher elevations.

Tuesday: Sunny in the morning, then partly cloudy with a chance of thunderstorms in the afternoon; highs 93-98 in the valleys and 77-87 at higher elevations. Partly to mostly cloudy with a chance of showers overnight; lows 57-67 in the valleys and 47-57 at higher elevations.

Wednesday: Partly cloudy in the morning, then mostly cloudy with a chance of showers and thunderstorms in the afternoon; highs 87-92 in the valleys and 73-83 at higher elevations. Mostly cloudy with a chance of showers and thunderstorms overnight; lows 55-65 in the valleys and 45-55 at higher elevations.

Thursday: Showers and thunderstorms likely; highs 81-86 in in the valleys and 68-78 at higher elevations. Showers and thunderstorms continue overnight; lows 81-86 in the valleys and 41-51 at higher elevations.

Friday: Showers and thunderstorms likely; highs 81-86 in in the valleys and 69-79 at higher elevations. Partly cloudy with a chance of showers and thunderstorms overnight; lows 52-62 in the valleys and 39-49 at higher elevations.

Saturday: Partly cloudy with a chance of showers and thunderstorms; highs 81-86 in the valleys and 69-79 at higher elevations. Partly cloudy with a chance of showers and thunderstorms overnight; lows 52-62 in the valleys and 39-49 at higher elevations.

What to pack, wear and do during a wildfire evacuation

The University of Nevada, Reno's Agriculture, Biotechnology and Natural Resources Extension created a peer-reviewed list of go-bag essentials.

The list includes:

Important documents such as insurance policies, medical records, birth certificates and banking info

ATM, credit and debit cards and cash in small bills

Medications, prescription (Rx) numbers and vaccination records (for people and pets)

Non-perishable food and bottled water for 72 hours

Driver’s license, passport and backup computer files or passwords

A home inventory (consider making a video inventory now, prior to an emergency)

Photographs of the exterior of the house and landscape

A printed address book with medical and veterinary contacts

Cell phone charger, car charger and battery packs

Toiletries and clothing for three to five days

Family heirlooms, photo albums and videos

Batteries

What should I wear during an evacuation?

If you’re ordered to evacuate due to wildfire, what you wear can reduce your risk of injury. The University of Nevada, Reno Extension recommends wearing only cotton or wool clothing — long pants, a long-sleeved shirt or jacket, a hat and boots — to help protect your skin from heat and embers.

The U.S. Department of Agriculture notes that natural fibers like cotton and wool char before they melt, unlike synthetic materials which can melt onto skin and cause severe burns.

UNR's Extension recommends carrying gloves and goggles. It also recommends wearing a NIOSH N95 or P100 mask, which will help filter out particulates and protect your lungs.

How can I plan when I might need to evacuate?

Before a wildfire threatens your area, it’s important to create a full evacuation plan — not just for yourself, but for your family, pets and home. The Extension recommends starting with the basics: Map out escape routes, choose a meeting point in case you’re separated and assign someone outside the area to help relay information.

Once you’ve laid that groundwork, you’ll need to consider the next steps — how to evacuate animals, what to do if you don’t drive, how to prep your home before leaving and how to know when it’s safe to return. Here’s how to build out that full plan:

Evacuating your family and making a plan

Before a wildfire is near, it’s important to make a detailed evacuation plan with your family. UNR’s Extension has several recommendations:

Plan multiple evacuation routes from your home

Designate a safe meeting place for everyone to congregate if you get separated

Assign a trusted contact to relay your evacuation plans

Register for a local emergency notification system like Reverse 911 or CodeRed You can also register in Washoe County's emergency database and keep it updated



If a fire is burning nearby and evacuation is likely, try to evacuate children, seniors or anyone who may need additional time or assistance first.

Evacuating your pets, livestock and other animals

If you have large animals or livestock, the Extension recommends having a trailer and reliable vehicle ready. Practice loading animals into the trailer before an emergency arises to reduce stress and ensure safety.

All animals should have some form of identification, such as a collar or microchip. Keep veterinary records and medications in a sealable, easy-to-grab bag stored in a central location.

Additional tips include:

Pack food, water and bowls in easy-to-carry, sealed containers

Assign each pet to a specific family member as part of a buddy system

Coordinate with neighbors who can help if you’re not home

Identify friends or relatives who can house your animals if you’re displaced. "This can be especially helpful for livestock and poultry," UNR's Extension said.

Secure a crate for each animal, with only one per carrier. Even calm pets may panic and try to escape during emergencies

If you must leave animals behind, notify your local animal control or emergency services immediately so they can attempt a rescue

Prepare your transportation for an evacuation

If you don’t drive, arrange transportation in advance with friends, neighbors or a local service.

If you do drive, take steps to ensure a fast and safe evacuation:

Keep your vehicle's gas tank full

Roll up the windows on your vehicle

Place essential items in the car

Park facing out of your driveway or garage

If parking in a garage, disconnect the electric door opener and lift the door manually

Close the garage door when you leave

Prepare your home during an evacuation

Before you leave your home during an evacuation, UNR's Extension recommends:

Closing all interior doors

Leaving a light on in each room

Removing lightweight, non-fire-resistant curtains and other combustible materials from around windows

Close fire-resistant drapes, shutters and blinds

Turn off all pilot lights

Move overstuffed furniture, such as couches and easy chairs, to the center of the room

Close fireplace damper

Close or block off any doggie-doors

Lock up firearms or valuables

Place combustible patio furniture and barbecues in the house, garage or away from the home

Shut off propane at the tank or natural gas at the meter, and clear the area of combustible material

Close all exterior vents, doors, and windows

Leave gates unlocked

Turn on outside lights

If available and if there’s time, cover windows, attic openings, and vents with plywood at least half an inch thick

Ensure that all garden hoses are connected to faucets and turned off

Don’t leave sprinklers or water running; doing so can reduce water pressure for firefighters

Ensure that house numbers and street signs are visible and reflective if possible

How do I know when to return home after an evacuation?

You can return home once local officials say the evacuation order has been lifted and it’s safe to do so. There are multiple ways you can keep up to date on fires and evacuation orders including:

Register for a local emergency notification system such as Reverse 911 or CodeRED

Visiting the Nevada Wildfire Information Dashboard at https://nifc.maps.arcgis.com/apps/dashboards/c205f43ea5df4f98b6d0f0f709d15e2f

Following Truckee Meadows Fire Protection District at https://x.com/TMFPD

Checking out https://inciweb.wildfire.gov/

Carly Sauvageau contributed to this report.

search_result.title: Reno Hawk Fire updates Monday: U.S. 395 opens, more ...
search_result.text:
Aug. 24, 2026 Updated Aug. 25, 2026, 9:38 a.m. ET

For the latest updates on the Hawk Fire on Tuesday, click here.

The Hawk Fire stands at a little over 15,000 acres burned, with evacuation orders in effect across northwest Reno and the North Valleys. Approximately 63,000 residents live within the mandatory evacuation and evacuation warning zones. The fire was listed at 27% containment as of 11 a.m. Monday.

A community meeting is scheduled for 7 p.m. Monday at the California Building at Idlewild Park, 75 Cowan Drive. It also will be livestreamed on RGJ.com.

Public safety officials have established an information line for the Hawk Fire at 775-244-6988. Information is also available at facebook.com/HawkFire2026.

Power restored to 3,000 customers, 7,000 still without

NV Energy has restored power to approximately 3,000 customers affected by the Hawk Fire. Approximately 7,000 electric customers and 250 gas customers remain de-energized.

Before power can be restored, NV Energy said crews must ensure conditions are safe.

Approximately 100 of the company’s structures were damaged or destroyed and 13 crews worked throughout the day to repair, rebuild and replace damaged poles and other equipment.

“Longer outages may be possible in areas where there was sustained damage to equipment that must be repaired,” NV Energy said in an email Monday evening.

U.S. 395 reopens, reduced evacuations for neighborhoods in North Valleys

U.S. 395 is now open to both northbound and southbound traffic, the Washoe County Sheriff's Office said Monday afternoon.

On-ramps and off-ramps are reopening, with the exception of access to North Virginia Street, which remains closed from Panther Drive to Village Parkway.

Evacuations on the east side of US 395 are also being downgraded from red “Evacuate Now” status to yellow “Get Set to Evacuate” in White Lake, Granite Hills, Granite Peak, North Valleys Regional Park and Alice Smith Elementary School area.

Several neighborhoods on the east side of US 395 will remain under the red "evacuate now" closure. This includes neighborhoods near Sierra Sage Golf course, Silver Lake Road and Moya Boulevard.

Please refer to perimetermap.com for the exact zones that are being downgraded.

"This remains a dynamic situation, and conditions can change quickly," the sheriff's office said in a Facebook post.

Residents are warned to use caution as they return home, as firefighters, law enforcement and other emergency personnel may be working in the area.

Smoke visible again Monday at 4 p.m.

The south side of Peavine in northwest Reno has a new plume of smoke Monday afternoon after looking quiet all day.

It comes as some fire evacuations were eased earlier on Monday.

Firefighters have warned conditions can change rapidly.

WCSD cancels school for second day because of Hawk Fire

The Washoe County School District canceled school on Tuesday, Aug. 25. It is the second day in a row schools are canceled because of the Hawk Fire.

All Reno and Sparks schools are closed. Incline and Gerlach schools will be open.

What to know about the Monday night fire spread risk

Reno Fire Division Chief Pete Bryant said at Monday's press conference that the Hawk Fire is 27% contained. The containment areas are along the southern portion of the incident, backing up to the Somersett area.

Bryant said where the fire jumped across U.S. 395 near Peppermint Drive on the east side of the road is also contained.

The cause of the fire is still under investigation. Truckee Meadows Fire Protection District Chief Richard Edwards said it is human-caused, but whether it was intentional is unknown.

"More than likely, this fire will be classified as undetermined," Edwards said.

The primary concerns for Monday night include the east side of the fire near North Valleys and the northwest side of the fire where there are more rugged mountain areas. Aviation resources are being used on both sides of the fire.

Bryant said there's always a potential the fire movement could be rapid, based on the weather conditions the area has had and what the area has experienced this summer.

"As we experienced with the Bug and Stallion (fires), one day it was looking really good, and by four o'clock, there was another huge column of smoke and flames coming down that we were dealing with," Bryant said.

"There is a threat. The threat has diminished significantly, but we really want to make sure that we're not putting people or responders at risk."

Bryant said the fire took off fast, covering a large amount of ground on multiple fronts over only 48 hours, which is part of the difficulty in communication efforts. He said the teams will do what they can to get information out as fast as possible.

63,000 still displaced, sheriff says 'lessons learned' with evacuations

TMFPD Chief Richard Edwards said 63,000 people are still displaced by the Hawk Fire.

Roughly 23,000 are in a "go now" red evacuation zone, and 40,000 are in a "get set" yellow evacuation zone.

Washoe County Sheriff Darin Balaam warns people to be cautious as roughly 23,000 residents return to their homes in Somersett.

"Go back into your neighborhoods," Balaam said. "But please do not go up into the burned areas. Fire is still in there, they're still moving their equipment."

Balaam also acknowledged that the fire moved rapidly, moving roughly 45 minutes from the top of Peavine Mountain to the Seneca Drive neighborhood. At the time, there was only one way in and out for residents trying to evacuate and fire teams trying to come in.

"We can do better, and we will," Balaam said. "We had all of the residents that were backed up trying to get out, and fire was going up and over all of their vehicles."

Balaam said they've been working with fire and road operations, and they will work on a better plan for getting evacuees out and getting fire equipment in. He said if they have to evacuate residents earlier in the next emergency they will, but that lessons were learned with these evacuations and routes.

Officials tell any evacuees that need additional resources to go to emergencywashoe.com.

NV Energy's Senior Vice President Jesse Murray said Somersett residents and residents near Mogul and Robb drives have power and gas, with the exception of three customers.

Roughly 10,000 North Valleys residents still do not have power, along with 250 customers who do not have gas service.

Murray said over 100 poles have been damaged, and NV Energy has 11 crews working to restore those damaged facilities. There is also damaged gas infrastructure near Seneca Drive that crews are working to restore.

No fatalities, 4 civilians injured, 3 minor firefighter injuries

TMFPD Fire Chief Richard Edwards said four civilians and three firefighters were injured from the Hawk Fire.

The three firefighters had minor burn injuries that happened during the initial fire attack. The status of the four injured civilians is unknown.

Multiple agencies have assisted with the Hawk Fire, including firefighters from 15 states, and international firefighters from Australia and New Zealand. Over 700 personnel are working on the Hawk Fire.

"They're very tired," Bryant said about the first responders.

Washoe County Sheriff Darin Balaam said one of his department's employees lost a home in the fire.

"A lot of them have been affected," Balaam said. "They are suffering, but the one thing is they are still coming everyday to serve this community."

Hawk Fire 27% contained, 32 homes destroyed, 6 damaged

The Hawk Fire has destroyed 32 homes and damaged six, fire officials said at a news conference at 2 p.m. Monday.

"We expect those numbers to increase as damage assessment teams are still out in the field assessing other areas right now," TMFPD Fire Chief Richard Edwards said.

The fire is 27% contained.

Somersett, Robb Drive evacuations downgraded

Areas in and around Somersett have been downgraded from red “Evacuate Now” status to yellow “Get Set to Evacuate,” including all neighborhoods off Robb Drive.

The road closures, including into Somersett are lifted.

While the evacuations have been downgraded, the Washoe County Sheriff said things can change quickly and this information comes soon after fire officials said winds could change the situation and the fire could grow later this afternoon.

While these areas have been downgraded to yellow "'Get Set to Evacuate status,' residents should remain vigilant, be prepared to evacuate if conditions change, and continue to closely monitor official updates," the sheriff's department said.

Hawk Fire could spread in next 12 to 48 hours

Fire officials said on Monday that the Hawk Fire is expected to make moderate to high intensity runs over the next 12 hours and possibly the next 48 hours.

"The fire has potential to spread northeast and northwest, and conditions remain dynamic and subject to rapid change," according to incident command.

As of Monday, 15,051 acres have burned since the fast moving fire started around 11:30 a.m. Aug. 22. The fire is 0% contained. It was human caused but no details have been given about what may have caused the fire to start.

In total, 720 people are working the fire that is being fueled by tall grass, brush and timber. Monday resources include 14 crews, 95 fire engines, 14 helicopters and 9 dozers.

Overnight, fire behavior was less extreme than anticipated in some areas, allowing crews to hold established lines and reposition resources to reinforce suppression efforts.

On the west side of the fire, firefighters are working to keep the fire out of Dog Valley and in flatter terrain. Crews working near the Somersett side of the fire constructed handlines with support from helicopters. Firefighters are also working around a natural gas line within the fire area. Mountainous terrain, continuous fuels and dry conditions continue to challenge suppression efforts

What roads, stores, banks are closed during evacuations

Many grocery stores, banks, and urgent care clinics remain closed during the evacuations.

Here’s what is closed as of Monday:

Renown’s urgent cares at North Hills and Northwest Reno locations

North Valleys Library

Peavine Animal Hospital

Raley’s in Lemmon Valley

Smith’s in Lemmon Valley

Grocery Outlet in Lemmon Valley

Walmart in Lemmon Valley

Greater Nevada Credit Union’s northwest Reno and Golden Valley branches

Great Basin Federal Credit Union’s North Valleys and Northwest Reno branches

Bank of America in Lemmon Valley

North Valley’s Regional Park

Current Hawk Fire road closure information

The following roads and U.S. 395 closures also remain in place:

Northbound U.S. 395 is closed from Parr Boulevard to Red Rock Road.

Southbound U.S. 395 traffic at Bordertown is being turned around before reaching White Lake.

Del Webb Parkway E and Somersett Parkway

Robb Drive and W 7th Street

N. Virginia and Panther Drive

N. Virginia and Golden Valley Road

Lemmon Drive at N. Virginia

North Hills Boulevard and Golden Valley Road

Beckwourth Drive and Golden Valley

10,000 people still without power

According to NV Energy, 9,854 residents are still without power in Washoe County. The majority of those outages are listed shutdowns because of an active wildfire and are in zip codes 89506 and 89508. Those zip codes are in the North Valleys. NV Energy does not have an estimate time for restoration.

Hawk Fire grows to more than 15,000 acres

The Hawk Fire has grown to more than 15,000 acres, according to a new fire perimeter from the National Interagency Fire Center.

The latest perimeter lists the fire at 15,040 acres, up from approximately 13,000 acres reported by fire officials Sunday morning.

An area of about 75 square miles remained under mandatory evacuation orders. Orders include parts of Somersett and neighborhoods north of West Seventh Street to North McCarran Boulevard. Residents should check perimetermap.com for exact boundaries and current road closures.

Options for Hawk Fire evacuees with children

Multiple Boys and Girls Clubs in Reno are offering child care on Monday for those affected by the Hawk Fire. Locations are open from 7 a.m. to 6 p.m.:

The Club at Pennington, 1300 Foster Drive

Donald W. Reynolds Youth & Teen Clubhouse, 2680 E. Ninth Street

Neil Road Youth Facility, 3905 Neil Road

Donald L. Carano Youth & Teen Clubhouse, 1090 Bresson Avenue

Reno Ice, 15500 Wedge Parkway in south Reno, is offering free public skate for those affected by the fire from 11:30 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. They are also allowing community members displaced to come into its rink from 5 a.m. to 10 p.m. if you need a cool place to relax for a few hours and need to charge your devices.

The Discovery, 490 S. Center Street in downtown Reno, said it is offering $5 admission for everyone on Monday. The museum is open from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m.

Hawk Fire community meeting set for 7 p.m. Monday

A community meeting to provide updates and information about the Hawk Fire is scheduled for Monday evening. The meeting is set for 7 p.m. in the California Building at Idlewild Park, 75 Cowan Drive in Reno.

Members of the public will have the opportunity to ask questions and share their concerns with public safety officials during the meeting.

The meeting also will be livestreamed on at facebook.com/hawkfire2026.

WCSD, TMCC classes canceled Monday due to Hawk Fire

WCSD: Classes have been canceled for nearly all Washoe County School District schools Monday due to the effects of the Hawk Fire, and Truckee Meadows Community College will be closed as well.

Parents of WCSD students were alerted via phone calls, texts and emails shortly after noon on Sunday.

"The decision to close schools is due to evacuations, impacts on regional public safety resources, and to help keep roads clear for emergency vehicles," the message read.

Gerlach K-12 School will hold classes as scheduled.

WCSD officials consulted with local law enforcement and public safety officials on the decision; the district cited strain on public safety and transit as crews continue to battle the fire.

"We understand that so many people in our WCSD family — students, families, and staff — are impacted," the message continued. "Over the next few days, we will continue to update our entire district family with information as it becomes available. We are grateful to our firefighters and first responders as they continue to battle this fire, and we thank our district personnel who are assisting with this effort."

TMCC: TMCC also canceled campus operations for Monday, including both in-person and remote classes, on what would have been the first day of instruction for the fall semester.

"Our thoughts are with everyone affected by the Hawk Fire and the extraordinary impact it is having across our region," the statement read. "With approximately 42,000 residents currently evacuated and another 45,000 residents in the evacuation warning areas, we know that many members of our TMCC community may be facing uncertainty, displacement or concern for family, friends, and neighbors."

TMCC's main campus at 7000 Dandini Boulevard is about one-half mile east of an evacuation warning zone.

University of Nevada, Reno: The University of Nevada, Reno, confirmed that it will continue ahead with its first day of class.

“Following an assessment of the Hawk Fire and current smoke conditions in the vicinity of the University of Nevada, Reno, the University has determined that regular campus operations will continue on Monday, Aug. 24,” UNR announced in a statement.

“Classes and operations at the University's main campus, Redfield campus and Lake Tahoe campus will proceed as scheduled.”

UNR added that it remains safe and is not located in either a red or yellow evacuation zone. The university also has an emergency response plan in place should the wildfire threaten the school.

“University leadership will continue to closely monitor fire activity, air quality conditions and guidance from local authorities, and will provide additional updates as needed,” UNR said.

Hawk Fire confirmed as human caused; 6 injured and 15,000 acres burned

The Reno area is grappling with another wildfire that was sparked by human hands, officials confirmed during a press event on Sunday morning.

“We can confirm that the fire was human caused,” said Shane Akerson, a battalion chief with the Truckee Meadows Fire Protection District.

“However, that is still undergoing active investigation and we don’t have further details provided at this time.”

Akerson also confirmed that the fire has grown from 10,500 acres late Saturday to approximately 15,000 acres as of late Sunday.

At least six injuries have been injured from the Hawk Fire so far — three civilians and three first responders, according to Akerson.

While officials confirmed that structures have been burned in the fire, they were unable to provide an exact count because the sites are not safe yet for investigators to enter.

About 800 personnel are working on the Hawk Fire as of Sunday morning, Akerson said.

The number of potentially affected residents by the Hawk Fire currently stands just under 90,000 people.

“Currently, we have 42,000 individuals who are placed on active evacuation, with approximately 45,000 individuals that are in the set status to be prepared to be evacuated,” Akerson said.

Slight chance of Monday afternoon showers near Hawk Fire

The National Weather Service predicted a slight chance of afternoon showers for the Reno, Sparks, Carson City and Minden area, which could aid firefighters in their efforts to slow the Hawk Fire.

The forecast called for partly cloudy conditions and patchy smoke on Monday, along with a slight chance of afternoon showers. Highs in the area are expected between 89 and 94, with light winds becoming southwest 10-15 mph winds in the afternoon.

Monday night's forecast predicted clear skies with patchy smoke, with the 10-15 mph winds decreasing overnight. Lows are expected to be between 56 and 66.

Partly cloudy and breezy conditions are expected for the area through Sunday, with another slight chance of showers on Friday afternoon.

Evacuation centers for Hawk Fire

Shelters have been set up for those under evacuation orders. Those include:

Evacuation center: Reno-Sparks Convention Center, Hall 4, 4590 S. Virginia Street

Access the evacuation center from Kietzke Lane and enter through Door 20F.

Please do not bring pets to the evacuation center.

Small animal evacuations: Washoe County Regional Animal Services, 2825 Longley Lane

Large animal evacuations: Ironwood Event Center, 5600 Whiskey Springs Road

Turn right into the second driveway. Please check in at the main office.

Evelyn Mount Northeast Community Center is no longer an evacuation shelter for the Hawk Fire.

Road closures due to Hawk Fire

Several main thoroughfares are closed to all traffic in and around the evacuation zones. As of 7:30 a.m. Sunday, those include:

U.S. 395 through the North Valleys is closed to all inbound traffic between Parr Boulevard and Bordertown.

search_result.title: Bug Fire Wednesday update: 9 WCSD schools to remain closed ...
search_result.text:
Aug. 12, 2026 Updated Aug. 13, 2026, 8:42 a.m. ET

For the latest updates on the Bug and Stallion fires on Thursday, Aug. 13, click here.

Ongoing wildfires north of Reno-Sparks have burned more than 100,000 acres since Saturday, forcing thousands of residents to evacuate a wide area stretching from the Nevada-California State Line to the shores of Pyramid Lake.

The Bug Fire, first reported Saturday, had grown to 70,766 acres as of 2 p.m. Wednesday, according to perimetermap.com. It has merged with the Fred Mountain Fire and stretched from U.S. 395 in California to Winnemucca Ranch Road in Nevada.

The Stallion Fire, a separate wildfire south of Pyramid Lake that started on Monday, also grew to 33,731 acres as of Wednesday afternoon.

The combined mandatory evacuation zone for the fires surpassed more than 500 square miles, with an additional 300 under evacuation warnings. Residents should rely on perimetermap.com for the most current evacuation information, including changes to evacuation status and repopulation.

Nine WCSD schools will remain closed Thursday

The Washoe County School District announced Thursday closures for nine schools in the area of ongoing wildfires. Those schools are:

Jesse Hall Elementary School

Desert Heights Elementary School

Lemmon Valley Elementary School

Natchez Elementary School

Silver Lake Elementary School

Spanish Springs Elementary School

Alyce Taylor Elementary School

Shaw Middle School

Spanish Springs High School

Natchez Elementary was in session on Monday, but classes there were canceled for Tuesday. All eight other schools on the list have yet to hold classes during the first week of the 2026-27 WCSD school year due to the wildfires.

395 closed at Nevada border

U.S. 395 is closed in both directions at the Nevada State Line to Doyle, California as the Bug Fire has flared again in some areas.

Despite rain in the region, motorists are being turned around at Hallelujah Junction, according to the Nevada State Police.

Evacuation warning, order areas extended north of Bug, Stallion fires

Additional evacuation orders and evacuation warnings have been issued on the northern side of the Stallion Fire and the Bug Fire.

As of Wednesday evening, the Bug Fire has burned 70,757 acres and is 3% contained[; 579 personnel are deployed.

The Stallion Fire is at 33,731 acres and 0% contained; 192 personnel are deployed.

'Notifications will start today to homeowners that have lost their homes'

The Bug and Stallion Fires have displaced over 5,100 people as of Wednesday afternoon, Washoe County Sheriff Darin Balaam said.

However, the sheriff reminded people they cannot go back to their homes, as the Nevada Guard and sheriff resources are at checkpoints and will turn people around.

“We are not trying to prevent those that are getting into their homes. We’re making sure they are safe, working with fire (officials) or is it safe to go in. Two days ago it looked like Red Rock was fine, then that night it ran all the way to Rancho Haven,” Balaam said.

“Please have patience. We understand the stress that everybody is under.”

The Bug Fire has grown to 70,757 acres, with 3% containment, and the Stallion Fire has grown to 33,730 acres with 0% containment.

Truckee Meadows Fire Protection District Fire Chief Richard Edwards also said there have been homes that were damaged and destroyed in the fire, and the notifications for lost homes will start today.

Washoe County’s emergency operation center will take the information from the home damage assessment teams, find the registered owner contact information, and they will call any homeowners who have had damaged or lost property.

Edwards also said if anyone has livestock left at their evacuated zones that they are trying to go back for, they are encouraged to call the Washoe County line 311 for help.

'Several more days' some NV Energy customers will be without power

Senior Vice President of NV Energy Jesse Murray also said roughly 1,200 people are still without power in Red Rock, Antelope Valley and Palomino Valley areas because this is where the active firefighting is occurring.

“The duration of the remaining outages at this time is unknown,” Murray said. “We do expect that restoration of some customers may take several more days.”

NV Energy will continue to evaluate areas they have to de-energize that are at risk in the fire zone, and areas that need to be re-energized as the fire risk moves away.

Rocky terrain makes for difficult situation for firefighters

The biggest concern for the fire’s direction going forward is growth in the northern areas up to Winnemucca Ranch Road for the Bug Fire, and the potential fire growth into the Palomino Valley from the Stallion Fire.

Ashleigh D’Antonio, operations section chief with the Southwest Area Complex Incident Management Team 1, said the terrain is exceptionally steep and rocky, making it difficult for heavy equipment and crews to get into, and she said their resources are already stretched thin.

"That Dogskin Mountain range is going to pose a huge problem and we really want to keep it from continuing north," D’Antonio. "And then just the fact that we are stretched very thin. We have about 100 firefighters per 30,000 acres of these fires."

But the National Weather Service is forecasting thunderstorms for the Reno-Sparks, Carson City and Minden areas, which can help douse fires with rain.

“Moisture is good. Rain is good,” D’Antonio said.

D’Antonio added that the southern flank of the Bug Fire is holding and contained, and evacuees may be able to go home soon.

“Based on our afternoon updates, we’re going to be coordinating with county sheriffs to start figuring out how we can let some folks back into that southern area,” D’Antonio said.

Rainfall sweeps through fire zone Wednesday afternoon

Sustained rain fell in the area of the Bug and Stallion fires as a band of storms moved over Reno-Sparks on Wednesday.

Fire crews have been keeping an eye on storms — both the moisture needed to fight the fire, and the wind and lightning strikes which could hamper efforts.

"Rain's great; higher humidity is great," Southwest Area Team One Operation Section Chief Ashley D'Antonio said of the afternoon rainshowers at a Wednesday press conference, "It will slow the fire progression and it will make it easier to actually attack the flanks."

More showers and thunderstorms are expected Wednesday through Friday, according to the National Weather Service:

Wednesday night: Mostly cloudy with a chance of showers and thunderstorms. Areas of smoke. Some thunderstorms may produce heavy rainfall. Lows 55 to 65. Southwest winds 10 to 15 mph.

Thursday: Showers likely and chance of thunderstorms. Areas of smoke. Some thunderstorms may produce heavy rainfall. Highs 78 to 83. Light winds becoming south around 10 mph in the afternoon.

Thursday night: Mostly cloudy with a chance of showers and thunderstorms in the evening, then partly cloudy after midnight. Areas of smoke through the night. Some thunderstorms may produce heavy rainfall in the evening. Lows 51 to 61. Southwest winds around 10 mph in the evening becoming light.

Friday: Sunny in the morning, then partly cloudy with a slight chance of showers in the afternoon. Highs 80 to 85. Light winds.

Friday night: Mostly cloudy with a chance of showers in the evening, then partly cloudy after midnight. Lows 51 to 61. West winds around 10 mph in the evening becoming light.

NV Energy restores power to some customers; nearly 1,200 still out of power

More than a thousand customers still have no power on Wednesday afternoon due to de-energizations of the grid in response to ongoing wildfires.

NV Energy restored power for about 240 customers in Nixon, which is being threatened by the Stallion Fire.

Approximately 1,198 customers are still without power, however, from emergency de-energizations as of 1:30 p.m. Wednesday, according to NV Energy. Power remains shut off for safety reasons in portions of Red Rock, Antelope Valley and Palomino Valley.

NV Energy does not have a time frame for when power is expected to be restored for affected customers, adding the power will be restored only when it is safe to do so.

Wildlife sanctuary Animal Ark evacuates animals from fire area

Animals at the Animal Ark Wildlife Sanctuary were safely evacuated Tuesday amid the threat of the Bug Fire north of Reno.

The Nevada Department of Wildlife said in a Facebook post Wednesday that their veterinarian and wildlife biologists helped Animal Ark staff safely evacuate one jaguar, three mountain lions, two bears, two wolves and one coyote.

“Moving large, potentially dangerous wildlife is no small task. To protect both the animals and the people handling them, the animals were temporarily immobilized before being carefully transported,” the post said.

Fire command post at Rancho San Rafael, rest of park remains open to public

Fire and police personnel are camped out at Rancho San Rafael Regional Park in Reno for the Bug and Stallion Fires on Wednesday.

The incident command post is on the west side of the park near the Coleman Drive entrance. This area is closed to the public and only allowing emergency vehicles in.

The Sierra Street and Washington Street entrances and the east side of the park are open to the public.

For Guard members fighting the fire in own neighborhoods, it's personal

The Nevada Guard’s Joint Staff Director Colonel Kyle Cerfoglio told the RGJ he understands residents' worries about evacuating, as his own home and many other emergency personnel’s homes sit in a “get set” evacuation zone.

Cerfoglio said he and his wife personalized a checklist of what to pack in their go-bags and helped his mother-in-law evacuate her large animals when she was put into a red zone.

“It kind of brings it home when you’re walking around your house saying what do I need, what’s irreplaceable,” Cerfoglio said. “It’s definitely an eerie feeling and I know it causes a ton of stress.”

And yet, the director is still on scene, with other guard members who live in the area.

Senior pilot instructor Scott Hermansen said one of their flight engineer’s homes was actively threatened in the neighborhood of Rancho Haven, off of Red Rock Road. Cerfoglio and Hermansen said the soldier happened to be assigned to fight the fire near there, and that it became a “personal mission” for him.

“We have members all over and there’s a lot that live out here in North Valleys and Cold Springs. It’s scary,” Cerfoglio said. “It’s definitely personal for all of us.”

Fire crews attack hot spots on Bug Fire; Stallion Fire continues spread

Fire crews directly engaged the fire Tuesday night to take advantage of cooler temperatures and higher humidity, according to the sheriff’s office.

Mop-up work has started at the south end of the Bug Fire with crews locating and extinguishing and remaining hot spots. Fire operations also strengthened control lines at the northern end of the Bug Fire while a dozer line was built on the west end at Rancho Haven, including an indirect line through the flats as the fire slowly backs down the Petersen Mountains.

The Stallion Fire grew on all sides, according to the sheriff’s office. Smoke from the Bug Fire and cloud cover, however, allowed crews to scout and build control lines while resources were used to defend the wildfire’s east side.

Resources being used to fight the wildfires and support ground crews include eight large air tankers, two very large air tankers, four water scoopers and several water-dropping helicopters.

The main focus yesterday for crews working on the Stallion Fire was to protect the community of Nixon, said Ashleigh D’Antonio, operations section chief with the Southwest Area Complex Incident Management Team 1.

“Yesterday we did have some perimeter growth pretty much all the way around (the Stallion Fire) except along the (State Route) 446 corridor,” D’Antonio said.

“We put in some direct line … to keep it out of Nixon and then wrapped it around a little bit to ensure that it stays in place while we work on the line construction for our features here above Palomino Valley.”

Although initial reports had the Bug Fire as high as 4% containment, both fires were listed at 0% containment as of 10 a.m. Wednesday.

“While the containment percentage has decreased, the primary objectives of preventing structure loss and ensuring public safety through coordinated, timely evacuations were achieved,” the Washoe County Sheriff’s Office said in a statement.

“Containment is measured against the full perimeter, and growth resets the percentage even where completed line continues to hold.”

Here's the most up-to-date map:

Boys & Girls Club offering free space for youth affected by wildfires

The Boys & Girls Club of Truckee Meadows is offering a free space for children affected by the wildfires burning in Northern Nevada.

The Boys & Girls Club is waiving its membership and weekly fees for ages 6 to 18 at its two clubhouses in Reno and Fernley.

“Our Fernley Clubhouse and William N. Pennington Youth & Teen Facility in Reno are open and available to provide … a safe, welcoming place while families navigate this difficult situation,” the Boys & Girls Club posted on its Facebook site.

“If you are looking for a safe place for your kids, please call or stop by our clubhouses.”

The Bug Fire and Stallion Fire have impacted many families in the area, with nine schools in Washoe County announcing that they will be closed Wednesday due to the wildfires.

Here is information about the two Boys & Girls Club facilities that are waiving fees:

William N. Pennington Youth & Teen Facility: Located at 1300 Foster Drive, Reno. The facility is open from 7 a.m. to 6 p.m. Details: 775-360-2469.

Located at 1300 Foster Drive, Reno. The facility is open from 7 a.m. to 6 p.m. Details: 775-360-2469. Fernley Clubhouse: Located at 695 E. Main St., Fernley. The facility is open from 7 a.m. to 6 p.m. Details: 775-460-4462

Nine schools to be closed Wednesday due to Bug, Stallion fires

The Washoe County School District on Tuesday evening announced Wednesday closures for nine schools in the area of ongoing wildfires. Those schools are:

Alyce Taylor Elementary School

Desert Heights Elementary School

Jesse Hall Elementary School

Lemmon Valley Elementary School

Natchez Elementary School

Silver Lake Elementary School

Spanish Springs Elementary School

Shaw Middle School

Spanish Springs High School

Natchez Elementary was in session on Monday, but classes there were canceled for Tuesday. All eight other schools on the list have yet to hold classes during the first week of the 2026-27 WCSD school year due to the wildfires.

Power shut down for 1,570 customers

Power remained out for thousands of customers in the North Valleys and near Pyramid Lake due to the wildfires, according to NV Energy.

The number of customers affected by outages in Washoe County started at 1,799 early Wednesday but has gone down to 1,570 as of 9 a.m.

NV Energy proactively cuts power in areas at risk from wildfires to reduce the risk of electric equipment causing secondary ignitions.

“The emergency de-energization was initiated on August 9 after the active wildfires posed a direct threat to electrical infrastructure,” NV Energy said in a statement. “The action was taken as part of NV Energy's comprehensive wildfire mitigation strategy to help reduce the risk of additional wildfire ignitions and protect public safety.”

Areas affected by de-energizations include Antelope Valley, Nixon, Palomino Valley and Sutcliffe. All customers impacted by the temporary shutdowns are in locations that are under evacuation orders or warnings, according to NV Energy.

NV Energy has not provided a timeline for when power will be restored to affected customers.

Evacuation center remains available at Evelyn Mount Community Center

The Washoe County Human Services Agency posted that it and American Red Cross of Nevada are ready to receive evacuees at the Evelyn Mount Community Center, 1301 Valley Road, Reno. They have beds, pillows, blankets, water, food and games.

Washoe County Regional Animal Services is accepting small animals at 2825 Longley Lane.

The large-animal shelter at the Reno-Sparks Livestock Events Center currently has more than 150 animals. Space and resources are limited, and residents who are able are encouraged to self-evacuate animals to a friend or family member’s home.

Churchill County is offering dry camping facilities and covered horse stalls at no charge for those evacuating local wildfires. The facilities are at the county's 3C Event Complex in Fallon, and are accessible at Miners Road off Sheckler Road. Water is available, but evacuees will need to provide their own feed for livestock.

Discounted hotel rooms are also available in the area for those needing to evacuate. This link offers a complete list: emergencywashoe.com/updates/.

Thunderstorms, flood watch in northwestern Nevada

Fire officials have been keeping an eye on thunderstorms moving into the area — especially wind and lightning, which may exacerbate the fires; and rain, which could assist fire suppression. Both are in the latest forecast for the Reno-Sparks, Carson City and Minden area.

“Today the rain and thunderstorm chances are the best just south of Reno and down into the eastern Sierra in Mono and also Mineral Counties,” said Mark Deutschendorf, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service in Reno.

“Not everyone’s going to get soaked with rain, but whenever storms pop up, there’s a risk of heavy rain.”

Heavy rain can also bring potential flooding, with a flash flood watch in effect for the Reno area from 2 p.m. Wednesday through 9 p.m. Thursday.

Winds are expected to be lighter today compared to recent days, at least until thunderstorms start, Deutschendorf said.

Here is the weather forecast for the area through Friday:

Wednesday: Mostly cloudy. Areas of smoke through the day. Chance of showers and thunderstorms in the afternoon. Some thunderstorms may produce heavy rainfall in the afternoon. Highs 88 to 93. Light winds becoming southwest around 10 mph in the afternoon.

Wednesday night: Areas of smoke in the evening. Mostly cloudy with a chance of showers and thunderstorms. Some thunderstorms may produce heavy rainfall. Lows 56 to 66. Southwest winds 10 to 15 mph.

Thursday: Showers likely and chance of thunderstorms. Areas of smoke in the afternoon. Some thunderstorms may produce heavy rainfall. Highs 80 to 85. Light winds becoming southwest around 10 mph in the afternoon.

Thursday night: Mostly cloudy with a chance of showers and thunderstorms in the evening, then partly cloudy after midnight. Some thunderstorms may produce heavy rainfall in the evening. Lows 51 to 61. Southwest winds around 10 mph in the evening becoming light.

Friday: Mostly sunny. Slight chance of showers in the afternoon. Highs 80 to 85. Light winds.

Friday night: Partly cloudy with a chance of showers in the evening, then clear after midnight. Lows 51 to 61.

UNR allowing staff, students affected by Bug Fire to go home

The University of Nevada, Reno, is allowing faculty, staff and students who live in areas affected by the Bug Fire to leave campus early and return home to prepare for evacuation.

“With the continued growth of the Bug Fire, faculty, staff and students with homes located within the ‘Yellow’ (Get Ready) evacuation zone have the flexibility to leave campus and return home to prepare for a possible evacuation,” the university posted on the UNR Bug Fire update page on Tuesday afternoon.

The second session and regular session of instruction for the summer ends on Wednesday, Aug. 12, with final grades for all summer classes due by 5 p.m. Friday, according to the UNR academic calendar.

Faculty and staff who need workplace accommodations due to the fire can reach out to their supervisor while students who need assistance can contact the Dean of Students Office (775) 682-6846.

The university’s leadership will continue to monitor the status of the fire and provide updates.

search_result.title: Oregon wildfire updates as blazes burn 1.5M acres, more homes lost
search_result.text:
Updated July 28, 2026, 3:09 p.m. ET

(This story has been updated to include additional information)

Oregon had 1.5 million acres of active wildfire burning July 28 mainly in central and eastern Oregon, and the 32 large wildfires have taken an increasing toll on the state.

A total of 23 homes have been lost so far while a few highways have remained closed — mainly near Prineville and Burns. Interstate 84 fully reopened between Baker City and Ontario late on July 27 after being closed by the Fox Fire.

Currently, Oregon has 12,200 fire personnel working the fires while the cost of suppression reached $144 million.

Here’s a roundup of notes and fire reports from across the state.

Hundreds of Salem-area campers evacuated from camp in central Oregon

Hundreds of teenagers from the Salem area were evacuated from a central Oregon summer camp as wildfires raged nearby on July 25.

Washington Family Ranch in Antelope evacuated 800 staff and campers during a Christian retreat. The group of campers included high schoolers from South Salem, Cascades, Sprague and West Salem, ranch spokesperson Gabe Knipp said.

The Little Buck Fire, part of the Hay Creek Fire Complex, quickly traveled toward the ranch July 25, reported the Statesman Journal’s Katie Livermore.

Advisory explains why Oregon wildfires are burning so aggressively

A new Pacific Northwest Fuels and Fire Behavior Advisory has been issued that helps explain why Oregon’s fires have been burning so aggressively this summer.

The advisory, produced by the U.S. Forest Service, says the winter’s low snowpack combined with recent drought “has led to live and dead fuels curing significantly earlier than usual,” the report said. “Fire activity is already reflecting patterns normally seen much later in the fire season. Alignment in the fire environment is producing extreme fire behavior.”

The area most impacted includes parts of the western Cascades but is much more focused on the central and eastern parts of the state, where the majority of the fires have been burning.

In looking forward, the advisory says the fires “are showing increased resistance to control, requiring more resources for longer periods and aviation support is often less effective,” the report said.

Feds approve 3 of 5 grants for wildfire emergencies

The Federal Emergency Management Agency approved three of five Oregon requests for Fire Management Assistance Grants. The grants are meant to provide financial assistance to state, local, tribal and territorial governments to help mitigate, manage and control active wildfires on public or private forests or grasslands that threaten to become major, a news release said.

The three approved were for Lower Dry Creek Fire near Milton-Freewater, the Awaka Butte Fire near Sisters and the Grasshopper fire near Pine Hollow.

It wasn’t clear what the two fires were that were declined assistance. The grants can pay for up to 75% of a state's eligible firefighting costs.

I-84 reopens but other highways still closed due to Oregon wildfires

A number of major highways are closed or partly closed across central and eastern Oregon on July 28 due to wildfires. They include:

U.S. Highway 20 between Burns and Ontario is closed

U.S. Highway 26 east of Prineville is closed

U.S. 30 south of The Dalles is closed

Fires force eastern, central Oregon into indefinite air quality advisory

There’s no end in sight for poor air quality in eastern and central Oregon.

The Oregon Department of Environmental has issued an air quality advisory, until further notice, for Baker, Crook, Gilliam, Grant, Harney, Jefferson, Malheur, Morrow, Umatilla, Union, Wallowa, Wasco and Wheeler counties due to smoke from nearly three dozen wildfires burning in the state.

It’s also warning of intermittent smoke in Deschutes, eastern Douglas, Hood River, northern Jackson, northern Klamath, Lake and Sherman counties. DEQ and partner agencies will reevaluate conditions on July 29, spokesman Dylan Darling said.

Castle Fire grows to 1,550 acres in Rogue-Umpqua Divide area

The lightning-ignited Castle Fire was mapped at 1,550 acres in Umpqua National Forest between Roseburg and Crater Lake, in the area near the Rogue-Umpqua Divide Wilderness area.

A type 3 incident management team is handling the blaze. Popular South Umpqua Falls Campground and Day Use Area was closed as of July 27. There is a wider closure around the area as well.

Full evacuation maps can be found using the RAPTOR mapping system.

Grasshopper Fire reaches 13,612 acres near Mount Hood

The Grasshopper Fire burning east of Mount Hood was mapped at 13,612 acres largely in the Badger Creek Wilderness. Fire crews held lines and were able to snuff out spot fires thrown off by the blaze on July 27, a morning report said.

Level 1, 2 and 3 evacuations were in place for the forest and Tygh Valley west of Maupin. The popular Flag Mountain Lookout site was wrapped in fire-resistant material by crews over the weekend.

Full evacuation maps can be found using the RAPTOR mapping system.

All of Oregon's wildfires will be updated as the information becomes available on July 28.

Bench Fire spreads both sides of Deschutes River, Lake Billy Chinook

A total of 11 homes have been lost in the Bench Fire burning near Warm Springs and Madras. On July 27, fire crews said that "most of Monday's activity was to the south and west toward populated areas on both sides of the Deschutes River and Lake Billy Chinook. There is high potential for further spread in this direction," wrote the Confederated Tribes of Warm Springs Fire Management.

Crews took direct suppression actions in the Campbell and Willow creeks and worked to prepare M-100, Highway 26 and 25 as part of the containment strategy.

Crews located and extinguished hot spots on Akawa Butte Fire near Sisters

Firefighters located hot spots with infrared detection equipment and are focused on extinguishing these areas of the Akawa Butte Fire, burning around 5 miles northeast of Sisters on July 28.

“Work on contingency lines is nearly completed. These lines are constructed as a secondary line of defense away from the main fire in case the fire crosses primary containment lines,” a morning report said.

The fire grew to 27,433 acres at 6% containment. Warm and dry conditions are expected to continue into this week without the high winds seen through the weekend.

Popular trails and recreation sites near Sisters were closed including: Black Butte Trail, Lower Black Butte Trailhead, Monty Campground, Perry South Campground, Indian Ford Campground, Green Ridge Lookout.

Levels 1, 2, and 3 evacuation orders remain in effect. Some areas around Indian Ford Road, Old Wagon Road, West Meadow Parkway, and Tumbleweed Turn were downgraded to a Level 2 evacuation order.

Fires merge in the 200,000 acre Rowe Creek Fire Complex, Fossil Bed closures remain

The Crosswhite, Brewer, and Green Mountain fires merged into one larger fire area on July 27 as crews continue to fight the Rowe Creek Fire Complex burning around 10 miles south of Fossil.

“Overnight infrared flight shows an increase in acreage due to the combined fire footprint, which lowers the overall containment,” a morning report July 28 said.

The complex was at 294,900 acres and 33% contained on July 28. Fire activity is anticipated to moderate, helping crews focus on the southwest corner of the incident, according to incident officials.

The Clarno and Painted Hills units of the Painted Hills Unit of John Day Fossil Beds National Monument remain closed. Level 1, 2, and 3 evacuation orders remain in place for areas in Wheeler and Wasco counties.

BLM-managed lands along both sides of the John Day River from Service Creek to the Columbia River remain closed.

Hay Creek Fire Complex near Antelope 90% contained

Crews have contained four of the five fires in the Hay Creek Fire Complex burning 10 miles north of Condon. The Little Buck Fire prompted new evacuations, including at Washington Family Ranch on July 25, but is now 50% contained.

Improved conditions reduced or lifted evacuation notices around the Hoag, Hopkin, Porcupine Ridge and Cottonwood fires. Oregon Route 218 and most of Cottonwood State Park reopened, according to a morning update.

The complex improved to 90% containment, according to the National Interagency Fire Center on July 28.

Crews made progress on the Coyote and Henry fires burning 15 miles southeast of Prineville

Three Level 3 evacuation zones to the south and east were downgraded to a Level 2 order on July 27 as firefighters made progress on the Coyote and Henry fires, located about 15 miles southeast of the Prineville Reservoir State Park.

The 17,480 acre Coyote Fire was at 63% containment, and the 29,489 acre Henry Fire was at 40% containment on July 28.

For the Coyote Fire, crews continued to build and strengthen containment lines. An Unmanned Aircraft System will check the fire perimeter heat signatures on July 28.

Crews focused efforts on containing the Henry Fire within Bedell Canyon to minimize impact on the Sand Hollow Wilderness Study Area.

Level 3 evacuation levels were in place around Maupin Butte as well as near Drake and Coyote Butte. All National Forest System lands, roads, and trails within the Maury Mountains remain closed.

Shingle Fire sees rapid growth near Mitchell, crews protect structures

The Shingle Fire burning around 13 miles southeast of Mitchell saw rapid growth over the weekend as challenging weather pushed the fire toward Highway 26 on July 26.

“An estimated 170 homes remain threatened as firefighters continue working to protect lives and property,” an evening report said on July 26.

The Shingle Fire grew to 63,253 acres and was 6% contained, according to the National Interagency Fire Center on July 28.

Level 2 and 3 evacuation orders were in place for areas around Table Mountain. Areas around the John Day Fossil Beds National Monument were under Level 1 and 2 evacuation orders

Second Flat Fire northeast of Highway 20 at 5% containment

The 92,443-acre Second Flat Fire, burning 6 miles northeast of Highway 20, was at 5% containment on July 28.

Firefighters are focused on protecting structures impacted by the fire and made progress on containment lines to the east and south on July 28. Crews aim to contain parts of the fire impacting communities in Hines and Burns.

Level 1, 2 and 3 evacuations remained for multiple areas of Harney County. Zones are searchable on the Genasys system online.

Hagan Fire near Tollgate grew to 29,267 acres

The Hagen Fire located about 9 miles southwest of Tollgate merged with the Ninemile Fire on July 26. On July 28, the fire remained uncontained at 29,267 acres.

“Firefighters are locating fire lines with the highest likelihood of stopping the spread of the fire to the east and south,” said a July 27 morning update.

Level 3, 2 and 1 evacuation orders remained for multiple areas of Umatilla County, searchable on the Genasys system online.

Containment 22% for Jackass Butte Fire near Harney Lake

Containment reduced to 22% on July 27 for the Jackass Butte Fire off Jackson Mountain Road. As the fire continues to approach containment lines, additional crews were assigned to the fire.

The fire grew to 22,123 acres on July 28 with no evacuation orders in place.

Fire crews are focused on preventing spread across Highway 205.

Hat Fire near Hat Butte 40% contained

The Hat Fire near Hat Butte was 40% contained on July 28 and at 42,500 acres.

No evacuation orders were in place.

Bald Mountain Fire spurs evacuation orders in areas of Harney County

Evacuation orders remained in areas of Harney County for the 32,137-acre Bald Mountain Fire, at 1% containment on July 28.

Crews worked to protect cabins and structures along Highway 78, including Riddle Road and Manns Lake Ranch. Weather conditions on July 28 are forecast to be favorable for fire suppression with higher humidity.

Level 3 and 1 evacuation zones are searchable on the Genasys system online.

Level 3 evacuation order issued for Juntura due to the uncontained Coleman Creek Fire

A Level 3 evacuation order was issued for Juntura and surrounding areas due to the 146,292-acre Coleman Creek Fire on July 27.

A California incident management team arrived to help on July 28.

Crews worked to keep the fire south of Highway 20 East and to secure the area near Riverside.

Level 3 and 2 evacuation orders for areas of Harney County are searchable on the Genasys system online.

Burnt Creek Fire uncontained near Enterprise

Crews have been successful to keep the Burnt Creek Fire, burning 33 miles north of Enterprise, from advancing further north on July 28, according to a morning update.

Officials noted that firefighting success has been partially due to a prescribed burn over a year ago which reduced available fuels.

The fire was at 3,117 acres with no containment on July 28.

A Level 1 evacuation order remained for all residents on Joseph Creek Road.

Evacuation orders remain for Big Grass Fire

Evacuation orders remained in place for the 196,962-acre Big Grass Fire burning near the eastern Oregon-Idaho state line. As of July 28, the fire was 5% contained.

A Level 3 evacuation order remained Pleasant Valley, South Mountain and Jordan Valley areas, as issued by the Owyhee County Sheriff’s Office on July 25. A Level 1 evacuation order remained for Triangle from Pleasant Valley Road, including Triangle Reservoir and Flint Creek Road area.

The sheriff’s office asked residents to use Bachman-Grade Road through Oreana in case of further evacuation notices.

Owyhee rangeland management specialists worked to assess fire impacts on livestock, including moving animals as needed, said the Bureau of Land Management Idaho. Affected landowners or permittees can contact the BLM Owyhee Field Office at (208) 896-5912.

Fox Fire near Huntington uncontained

The 58,049-acre Fox Fire near Huntington spread south and remained uncontained on July 28.

Interstate 84 in eastern Oregon reopened between Baker City and Ontario after closing on July 27 due to the fire. As crews work to protect structures, powerlines, gas lines and railroads along I-84, officials asked motorists to slow down to make space for emergency vehicles.

As winds are expected to move the fire northwest on July 28, crews plan to use roads and creeks to steer the fire toward Lookout Mountain, according to a morning update.

Level 2 and 3 evacuation orders for areas of Baker County remained near Morgan Mountain and Brownlee Reservoir, searchable on the Genasys system online.
